lessons.title: Proof by induction
notes: Induction proves a statement for an infinite sequence of integer values using a base case and a conditional step. State the starting integer, assume the exact proposition for k, and use that assumption to establish the proposition for k + 1. The assumption is a temporary hypothesis, not the conclusion.

For sums, add the new term to the assumed formula. For divisibility, separate the new expression into a multiple of the assumed expression and an explicitly divisible remainder. For matrix powers, multiply in the correct order. Finish by stating that the base case and implication establish the result for all integers in the stated domain.

example.q: Prove 1 + 3 + … + (2n − 1) = n² for n ≥ 1.
steps: Assume the sum to k equals k².
The sum to k + 1 is k² + (2k + 1).
The statement holds for n = 1 and propagates from k to k + 1, so it holds for all integers n ≥ 1.

practice.q: Prove that 3ⁿ − 1 is divisible by 2 for every integer n ≥ 1.

check.q: Using 1+3+…+(2n−1)=n², what is the sum when n=6?

deep.tip: State the proposition for n = k exactly as given, and make the step where the assumption is used visible. A proof that never uses the inductive hypothesis is not a proof by induction. Finish with a conclusion that mentions the base case, the step and the set of integers covered.

examples.title: Divisibility
examples.q: Prove by induction that 7ⁿ − 1 is divisible by 6 for all positive integers n.
steps: True for n = 1, and true for n = k implies true for n = k + 1, so true for all positive integers n.

examples.title: A matrix power
examples.q: Prove by induction that [[1,1],[0,1]]ⁿ = [[1,n],[0,1]] for all positive integers n.
steps: This is the stated result with n = k + 1.
True for n = 1 and the step holds, so the result is true for all positive integers n.

examples.title: A sum with a product term
examples.q: Prove by induction that Σ r(r + 1) from r = 1 to n equals n(n + 1)(n + 2)/3.
steps: Assume the sum to k is k(k + 1)(k + 2)/3.
This is the formula with n = k + 1; with the base case, it holds for all positive integers n.

parts.q: Prove by induction that, for all positive integers n, Σ r³ from r = 1 to n equals n²(n + 1)²/4.
ms: assumes true for n = k and adds (k + 1)³
complete conclusion: base case, inductive step, all positive integers

exam.stem: f(n) = 4ⁿ + 6n − 1, where n is a positive integer.

parts.q: Find f(1) and f(2).
Prove by induction that f(n) is divisible by 9 for all positive integers n.
ms: conclusion using f(1) = 9 as the base case

exam.stem: A sequence is defined by u₁ = 5 and uₙ₊₁ = 3uₙ − 4.

parts.q: Find u₂ and u₃.
Prove by induction that uₙ = 3ⁿ + 2.
ms: assumes uₖ = 3ᵏ + 2 and substitutes into uₖ₊₁ = 3uₖ − 4

lessons.title: Complex arithmetic and polynomial roots
notes: The imaginary unit satisfies i² = −1. Combine real and imaginary parts separately in addition, and expand products before replacing i². To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator; the denominator becomes a real modulus squared.

A polynomial with real coefficients has non-real roots in conjugate pairs. This conclusion depends on real coefficients: it is not true for an arbitrary complex-coefficient polynomial. A quadratic with negative discriminant still has two complex roots. Check a proposed root by substitution rather than by its appearance.

example.q: Solve z² − 4z + 13 = 0 and calculate the product of the roots.
steps: The product is 13, agreeing with the constant term.

practice.q: Simplify (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i), giving a + bi.

check.q: What is i²?

deep.tip: Decide first whether the coefficients are real: only then do non-real roots come in conjugate pairs. When dividing, write the conjugate multiplication as a separate line so the real denominator is visible, and when finding square roots keep both sign choices until the final line.

examples.title: Using a given complex root
examples.q: Given that 1 + 2i is a root of z³ − 5z² + 11z − 15 = 0, solve the equation completely.
steps: Real coefficients, so 1 − 2i is also a root.
z³ − 5z² + 11z − 15 = (z² − 2z + 5)(z − 3), comparing the z³ and constant terms.

examples.title: Square roots of a complex number
examples.q: Find the square roots of 5 − 12i.
steps: Let (a + bi)² = 5 − 12i with a, b real.
Real and imaginary parts: a² − b² = 5 and 2ab = −12.
a is real, so a = ±3 and b = ∓2.

exam.stem: f(z) = z⁴ − 6z³ + 23z² − 34z + 26. Given that 1 + i is a root of f(z) = 0:

parts.q: write down another complex root;
solve f(z) = 0 completely.
ms: divides or compares coefficients to find the other quadratic factor

exam.stem: The complex number z satisfies (2 − i)z = 7 + 4i.

parts.q: Find z in the form a + bi.
ms: multiplies numerator and denominator by 2 + i

parts.q: z is a root of z² + pz + q = 0, where p and q are real. Find p and q.
ms: uses the conjugate root 2 − 3i: sum 4, product 13

parts.q: Find the square roots of −7 + 24i.

lessons.title: Argand diagrams, loci and regions
notes: An Argand point represents z = x + iy by coordinates (x,y). The distance |z − a| is the distance from the point for z to the point for a. Equality of distances gives a perpendicular bisector; a fixed distance gives a circle. An argument condition fixes a directed angle and usually describes a ray, not an entire line.

Use an algebraic equation to check the geometry, and distinguish boundaries included by ≤ from boundaries excluded by <. The argument of zero is undefined, so a point making the argument expression zero is excluded. Intersections of regions must satisfy every original condition.

example.q: Describe |z − (2 + i)| = 3 and |z − 1| = |z + 3|.
steps: The first locus is a circle with centre (2,1) and radius 3.
For the second, points are equally far from (1,0) and (−3,0).
Algebra confirms (x − 1)² + y² = (x + 3)² + y² gives x = −1.

practice.q: Describe the locus |z − (1 − 2i)| = 4 and determine whether z = 1 + 2i lies on it.
steps: At z = 1 + 2i the distance from the centre is 4.
The point lies on the circle.
A correct sketch labels both axes, centre and radius.

check.q: What is the radius of |z−(2+i)|=3?

deep.tip: Translate each condition into geometry before any algebra: |z − a| is a distance from the point a, and arg(z − a) is a direction measured at a. Mark the fixed points first, state whether each boundary is included, and remember that a half-line from an arg condition does not include its starting point.

examples.title: Greatest and least modulus on a circle
examples.q: z satisfies |z − 3 − 4i| = 2. Find the least and greatest values of |z|.
steps: The locus is a circle, centre (3, 4), radius 2.
The centre is √(3² + 4²) = 5 from the origin.
The nearest and farthest points lie on the line through the origin and the centre.

examples.title: A half-line
examples.q: Sketch the locus arg(z + 1 − i) = 3π/4 and give its Cartesian equation.
steps: Write as arg(z − (−1 + i)) = 3π/4: a half-line starting at (−1, 1).
The direction 3π/4 has gradient tan(3π/4) = −1 and points up and to the left.
The locus is y = −x for x < −1; the point (−1, 1) itself is excluded (open circle).

examples.title: Area of a region
examples.q: Find the area of the region defined by |z − 2| ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ arg z ≤ π/4.
steps: The circle has centre (2, 0) and radius 2, so it passes through the origin; in polar form r = 4cos θ.
The region is swept out from the origin for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.
Area = ½∫ 16cos²θ dθ = 4∫ (1 + cos 2θ) dθ from 0 to π/4.

exam.stem: The complex number z satisfies |z + 2 − 2i| = √2.

parts.q: Describe the locus of z.
Find the greatest value of |z|.
ms: distance of the centre from O is 2√2, then adds the radius

parts.q: Find the greatest value of arg z, where −π < arg z ≤ π.
ms: uses the tangent from O: right angle between tangent and radius

exam.stem: The region R is defined by |z| ≤ 4 and π/6 ≤ arg z ≤ π/2.

parts.q: Find the exact area of R.
ms: R is a sector of the circle centre O, radius 4

exam.stem: The complex number z satisfies |z − 6| = |z − 2i|.

parts.q: Find a Cartesian equation of the locus of z.
Find the least value of |z|.
ms: perpendicular distance from O to 3x − y − 8 = 0

lessons.title: Modulus, argument and exponential form
notes: For z = x + iy, the modulus is √(x² + y²); choose the argument using the quadrant as well as a tangent ratio. Euler form z = re^(iθ) makes multiplication and division geometric: multiply or divide moduli and add or subtract arguments.

Principal arguments are normally chosen in (−π,π]. Angles differing by 2π represent the same non-zero complex number. An exponential-form calculation must preserve the modulus; addition is generally easier in Cartesian form and does not add moduli and arguments separately.

example.q: Write −1 + i in exponential form and square it.
steps: The point is in quadrant II, so arg z = 3π/4.

practice.q: Write −√3 − i in modulus-argument form.
steps: The point lies in quadrant III.

check.q: What is the modulus of −3+4i?

deep.tip: Plot the number before quoting an argument: the quadrant decides the angle, not the calculator value of arctan. Use exponential or modulus-argument form for products, quotients and powers, Cartesian form for sums, and bring every final argument back into (−π, π].

examples.title: Products and quotients
examples.q: z = 2e^(iπ/3) and w = 3e^(−iπ/4). Find zw and z/w in the form re^(iθ) with −π < θ ≤ π.
steps: Multiply moduli and add arguments: zw = 6e^(i(π/3 − π/4)).
Divide moduli and subtract arguments: z/w = (2/3)e^(i(π/3 + π/4)).

examples.title: A power in Cartesian form
examples.q: Find (1 + i√3)⁶ in the form a + bi.
steps: |1 + i√3| = 2 and the point is in the first quadrant with arg = π/3.

fills.q: Argument of a point on the negative imaginary axis.

parts.q: Find the modulus and the argument of z.
ms: uses arctan(√3) with z in the second quadrant

parts.q: Find z⁴ in the form a + bi.

exam.stem: z = 4(cos π/6 + i sin π/6) and w = 2(cos(−π/3) + i sin(−π/3)).

parts.q: Find zw in modulus-argument form.
Find z/w in the form a + bi.
Find |w| and arg w, giving exact answers.
ms: divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments

lessons.title: De Moivre, roots of unity and trigonometric identities
notes: For an integer n, [r(cosθ + i sinθ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ). To find all nth roots, use every angle (θ + 2kπ)/n for k = 0,…,n − 1. These points are equally spaced on a circle, and omitting the 2kπ term loses roots.

Expand (cosθ + i sinθ)ⁿ and compare real and imaginary parts to derive identities. For powers of sine and cosine, Euler forms convert products to sums of exponentials; pair conjugate terms to obtain a real result. Check the number of distinct roots and the modulus of each.

example.q: Find all cube roots of 8.
steps: Each cube root has modulus 2 and angle 2kπ/3.
For k = 0,1,2, the roots are 2, −1 + √3 i, −1 − √3 i.
Cubing each gives 8; the roots are 120° apart.

practice.q: Find all fourth roots of −16.
steps: The roots are ±√2 ± √2 i, with all four sign combinations.
Plot four equally spaced points on the circle of radius 2.

check.q: How many distinct fifth roots does a non-zero complex number have?

deep.tip: For roots, write the right-hand side with its general argument θ + 2kπ before dividing by n, and list exactly n values of k. For identities, decide whether you need real or imaginary parts before expanding, and convert everything to one trigonometric function at the end.

examples.title: A multiple-angle identity
examples.q: Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ.
steps: (cos θ + i sin θ)³ = cos 3θ + i sin 3θ.
Expanding with c = cos θ, s = sin θ: c³ + 3ic²s − 3cs² − is³.
Replace s² by 1 − c²: cos 3θ = c³ − 3c(1 − c²).

examples.title: Fourth roots
examples.q: Solve z⁴ = 8 + 8√3 i, giving the roots in the form re^(iθ) with −π < θ ≤ π.
steps: |8 + 8√3 i| = 16 and the argument is π/3.

examples.title: A power of sine
examples.q: Express sin⁴θ in terms of cos 4θ and cos 2θ.
steps: With z = e^(iθ): z − 1/z = 2i sin θ and zⁿ + 1/zⁿ = 2cos nθ.

lines: (cos θ + i sin θ)⁵ = cos [[5]]θ + i sin [[5]]θ
the sum of the n distinct nth roots of unity is [[0]]

parts.q: Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that sin 5θ = 16sin⁵θ − 20sin³θ + 5sin θ.
ms: expands (c + is)⁵ with the binomial theorem

parts.q: Hence find all the solutions of 16x⁵ − 20x³ + 5x = 0, giving non-zero roots to 3 decimal places.
ms: sets x = sin θ and solves sin 5θ = 0

parts.q: Solve z³ = −8i, giving the roots in the form re^(iθ) with −π < θ ≤ π.
The roots are the vertices of a triangle in the Argand diagram. Find its exact area.
ms: equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius 2: side 2√3

parts.q: Show that 1 + ω + ω² + ω³ + ω⁴ = 0.
ms: ω⁵ = 1 and ω ≠ 1, so the sum is 0

parts.q: Hence find the exact value of cos(2π/5) + cos(4π/5).

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication, determinants and inverses
notes: A matrix product is defined only when the inner dimensions agree. Each entry is a row–column dot product, so AB and BA need not agree. The determinant of a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] is ad − bc; an inverse exists only when this is non-zero.

For a 3×3 determinant, expand along a convenient row or column with alternating cofactor signs. Transpose the cofactor matrix to form the adjugate, then divide by the determinant. Check an inverse by multiplying to obtain I; a singular matrix cannot be rescued by dividing by zero.

example.q: Find the inverse of A = [[2,1],[3,2]].
steps: Swap diagonal entries and negate the other two.

practice.q: Find the determinant and inverse of B = [[3,1],[2,1]].
steps: State that the non-zero determinant guarantees an inverse.

deep.tip: Check that the dimensions allow the product and keep the order: AB ≠ BA in general and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. For a 3 × 3 inverse, lay out minors, then cofactor signs, then the transpose, and confirm one row of AA⁻¹ before using the result.

examples.title: A singular 3 × 3 matrix
examples.q: A = [[1,2,0],[3,−1,2],[1,0,k]]. Find the value of k for which A is singular.
steps: Expand along the first row: det A = 1(−k − 0) − 2(3k − 2) + 0.
A is singular when det A = 0.

examples.title: Inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix
steps: Transpose and divide by 3: M⁻¹ = ⅓[[1,1,−1],[−1,2,1],[1,−2,2]].
Check the first row of MM⁻¹: ⅓(2 + 1, 2 − 2, −2 + 2) = (1, 0, 0).

fills.q: Determinant of a product, with det A = 3 and det B = −2.

exam.stem: M = [[k,2],[3,k − 1]], where k is a constant.

parts.q: Find the values of k for which M is singular.
Given that k = 4, find M⁻¹.
ms: det M = 6 and swaps/negates the entries

parts.q: Find det A.
Find A⁻¹.
ms: transposes and divides by det A

parts.q: Hence solve x + 2z = 5, 2x + y = 4, 3y + z = 8.
Find the matrix B.
ms: B = A⁻¹(AB), multiplying on the left

lessons.title: Linear transformations and invariant objects
notes: The columns of a 2D transformation matrix are the images of the standard basis vectors. If B acts first and A second, the composite matrix is AB. A determinant gives signed area scale factor: its magnitude scales area and its sign records orientation.

An invariant point satisfies Mx = x. A line can be invariant without every point on it being fixed. To test a proposed invariant line, transform a general point on the line and check that its image still satisfies the line equation. Rotations, reflections, stretches and shears should be interpreted geometrically as well as algebraically.

example.q: For M = [[1,2],[0,1]], describe the transformation and find its invariant points.
steps: This is a shear parallel to the x-axis, with shear factor 2.
Invariant points satisfy x + 2y = x, so y = 0.
Every point on the x-axis is fixed; det M = 1 preserves area.

practice.q: A maps (x,y) to (−y,x). Write A and find A².
steps: These represent anticlockwise 90° and 180° rotations about the origin.

check.q: For the shear (x,y)↦(x+2y,y), find the first coordinate of the image of (1,3).

deep.tip: Read a matrix through its columns, the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1), and write composites right to left: the first transformation is the right-hand factor. For an invariant line, transform a general point (t, mt + c) and require the image to satisfy the same equation; do not confuse this with a line of invariant points.

examples.title: Invariant lines through the origin
examples.q: Find the invariant lines through the origin for M = [[4,−2],[1,1]].
steps: A general point on y = mx is (t, mt); its image is (4t − 2mt, t + mt).
The image lies on y = mx when t + mt = m(4t − 2mt).
The invariant lines are y = ½x and y = x.

examples.title: A composite transformation
examples.q: R is a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about O and S is a reflection in y = x. Find the single transformation equivalent to R followed by S.
steps: R followed by S is the product SR.
This is a reflection in the x-axis.

examples.title: Area scale factor
examples.q: A triangle of area 5 is transformed by [[3,1],[2,4]]. Find the area of its image.
steps: Image area = 5 × 10 = 50; the positive determinant means orientation is preserved.

parts.q: Describe fully the transformation represented by A.
Explain why A⁸ = I.
ms: eight rotations of 45° make a full turn of 360°

parts.q: Find the matrix representing A followed by B.
Show that the line y = x is invariant under T.
ms: the image lies on y = x, so the line maps to itself

parts.q: Find the other invariant line through the origin.
State, with a reason, whether y = x is a line of invariant points.
ms: no: (t, t) maps to (5t, 5t), so only the origin is fixed

parts.q: The triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 3) is transformed by [[2,−1],[3,5]]. Find the area of the image.

lessons.title: Three-equation systems and singular geometry
notes: Write a linear system as Ax = b and use elimination or a matrix inverse when available. A zero determinant means a unique solution is not guaranteed: the system may be inconsistent or may have infinitely many solutions. Compare augmented rows to distinguish these cases.

In three dimensions, each linear equation represents a plane. Three planes may meet at one point, share a line or plane, or have no common point. A determinant calculation alone does not distinguish an empty intersection from a non-unique intersection; interpret the equations and any free parameter.

example.q: Solve x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, and 2x + y − z = 3.
steps: Subtract the second equation from the first: 2y = 4, so y = 2.
Substitute all three values in the original equations.

practice.q: Explain the solution set of x + y + z = 2 and 2x + 2y + 2z = 5.
steps: The planes are parallel and distinct.

check.q: If x+y+z=6 and x−y+z=2, what is y?

deep.tip: Find the determinant first: non-zero means one point, zero means you must test consistency. When the determinant is zero, combine the equations to see whether they agree (a line or plane of solutions) or contradict (no common point), and name the configuration: sheaf, prism, or parallel planes.

examples.title: A parameter and a sheaf
examples.q: x + 2y − z = 3, 2x − y + 3z = 4 and 3x + y + 2z = k. Find k for which the equations are consistent and interpret the result.
steps: The left side of the third equation is the sum of the first two left sides.
So the coefficient determinant is 0: there is no unique solution.
Adding the first two equations gives 3x + y + 2z = 7.
The system is consistent only when k = 7.
For k = 7 the three planes form a sheaf, meeting in a line; otherwise they form a triangular prism with no common point.

examples.title: A unique solution by elimination
examples.q: Solve 2x + y − z = 1, x − y + 2z = 5 and 3x + 2y + z = 10.
steps: Add the first two equations: 3x + z = 6.
Twice the second plus the third: 5x + 5z = 20, so x + z = 4.
(x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3); check in the third: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10.

fills.q: Two equations: x + y = 5 and x − y = 1.
The planes x + y + z = 1 and x + y + z = 4.

exam.stem: The equations x + y + 2z = 4, 2x − y + z = 3 and 3x + az = b are given, where a and b are constants.

parts.q: Find the determinant of the coefficient matrix in terms of a.
State the value of a for which there is no unique solution.
Given a = 3 and b = 7, show that the equations are consistent and interpret this geometrically.
ms: this is the third equation, so the system is consistent
the three planes form a sheaf: they meet in a line

parts.q: Solve the simultaneous equations x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + 3z = 9 and x + 2y − z = 2.
ms: eliminates one variable from two pairs of equations

exam.stem: Π₁: x − 2y + z = 3, Π₂: 2x − 4y + 2z = 1 and Π₃: x + y − z = 0.

parts.q: Describe the configuration of the three planes.
ms: Π₁ and Π₂ are parallel and distinct: normals proportional, constants not
no common point; Π₃ cuts them in two parallel lines

lessons.title: Polynomial roots and transformations of roots
notes: For a monic cubic with roots α, β, γ, the coefficients give α+β+γ, αβ+βγ+γα and αβγ with alternating signs. Use these relations to build a polynomial or evaluate symmetric expressions without solving the original equation.

If new roots are a transformation of the old ones, introduce a new variable and substitute its inverse relation into the original polynomial. Clear denominators and check degree and leading coefficient. Squaring a sum includes cross terms; Σα² is not (Σα)².

example.q: Roots α,β,γ satisfy x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = 0. Find α² + β² + γ².

practice.q: Find a monic polynomial whose roots are twice the roots of x³ − 3x + 1 = 0.
steps: The degree and number of roots are unchanged.

check.q: For roots of x³−6x²+11x−6=0, what is their sum?

deep.tip: Write the equation with its leading coefficient visible before quoting sums and products, since each is divided by that coefficient and the signs alternate. For a transformed equation, substitute the inverse relationship and clear fractions; for powers of roots, use the equation itself to reduce α³ rather than expanding brackets.

examples.title: Symmetric functions of a cubic
examples.q: α, β, γ are the roots of 2x³ − 5x² + 4x − 3 = 0. Find Σ1/α and Σα².

examples.title: A linear transformation of the roots
examples.q: The roots of x³ − 3x² + 4 = 0 are α, β, γ. Find the cubic with roots α + 2, β + 2, γ + 2.
steps: Let w = x + 2, so x = w − 2.
Check: the sum of the new roots is 3 + 6 = 9, matching the w² coefficient.

examples.title: What a sum of squares can show
examples.q: α, β, γ, δ are the roots of x⁴ − 2x³ + 3x² + 4x − 5 = 0. Find Σα² and explain what it shows.
steps: A sum of squares of real numbers cannot be negative, so the roots are not all real.

exam.stem: The roots of x³ + 2x² − 3x + 4 = 0 are α, β and γ.

parts.q: Write down the values of α + β + γ, αβ + βγ + γα and αβγ.
Find α² + β² + γ².
Find α³ + β³ + γ³.

exam.stem: The roots of x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0 are α, β and γ.

parts.q: Find a cubic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are 2α − 1, 2β − 1 and 2γ − 1.

exam.stem: The roots of 2x² − 6x + 7 = 0 are α and β.

parts.q: Find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are α² and β².

lessons.title: Power sums and the method of differences
notes: Use standard sums of r, r² and r³ to simplify a polynomial term before summing. The method of differences works by expressing a term as consecutive differences; nearly all interior terms then cancel. Write the first few and last few terms so the uncancelled endpoints are visible.

Partial fractions can reveal a telescoping form. A finite identity and an infinite sum are different statements: to pass to infinity, show that the remaining endpoint tends to a finite limit. Keep the starting index consistent.

example.q: Find the sum from r = 1 to n of 1/[r(r + 1)].
steps: The sum is n/(n + 1); its limit is 1.

practice.q: Find the sum from r = 1 to n of 2r² + 3r.

check.q: Find Σr from r=1 to 10.

deep.tip: Split a polynomial summand into standard sums and factorise as early as possible: n(n + 1) is almost always a common factor. For the method of differences, write out the first two and last two rows so the cancelling pattern is visible, and check the final formula with n = 1.

examples.title: Standard results
examples.q: Show that Σ r(2r − 1) from r = 1 to n equals n(n + 1)(4n − 1)/6.

examples.title: Method of differences
examples.q: Find Σ 2/[(2r − 1)(2r + 1)] from r = 1 to n.

examples.title: A sum that does not start at 1
examples.q: Find Σ r² from r = n + 1 to 2n in factorised form.
steps: Sum = S(2n) − S(n), where S(n) = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.

parts.q: Show that Σ r(r + 3) from r = 1 to n equals n(n + 1)(n + 5)/3.
Hence evaluate Σ r(r + 3) from r = 11 to 30.
Express 1/[r(r + 2)] in partial fractions.
Hence show that Σ 1/[r(r + 2)] from r = 1 to n equals ¾ − (2n + 3)/[2(n + 1)(n + 2)].
ms: writes out the first and last terms
identifies the terms that do not cancel

parts.q: State the sum to infinity.
Show that Σ (r³ − r) from r = 1 to n equals ¼(n − 1)n(n + 1)(n + 2).

lessons.title: Maclaurin expansions and approximation
notes: A Maclaurin expansion uses derivatives at zero: f(0)+f′(0)x+f″(0)x²/2!+… . Recognise the expansions of eˣ, sin x, cos x and ln(1+x), and substitute a complete expression carefully into a known series. Calculate derivatives through the requested order before evaluating them at zero.

A truncated series approximates a function near its expansion point. State the terms retained and any domain or convergence restriction. Terms with the same power must be collected after multiplying series, and powers discarded only after all products contributing to the requested order have been included.

example.q: Expand e^(2x) through the x³ term.
steps: At x = 0.05, the cubic approximation is 1.105166… .

practice.q: Expand sin(2x) through the x⁵ term.
steps: Use sin u = u − u³/6 + u⁵/120 + … .
The approximation is local to x = 0.

check.q: What is the coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin expansion of e^(2x)?

deep.tip: Decide whether to differentiate repeatedly or to build the series from standard results: a composite of standard functions is usually quicker by substitution. Keep terms only up to the required power when multiplying, and quote the interval of validity when a logarithm or binomial series is involved.

examples.title: A logarithmic series
examples.q: Find the Maclaurin series for ln(1 + 2x) up to the term in x³, stating the values of x for which it is valid.
steps: ln(1 + u) = u − u²/2 + u³/3 − …, valid for −1 < u ≤ 1.
Valid when −1 < 2x ≤ 1, that is −½ < x ≤ ½.

examples.title: Multiplying two series
examples.q: Find the series expansion of eˣ cos x up to the term in x³.
steps: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6 + … and cos x = 1 − x²/2 + …
Multiply, keeping terms up to x³: (1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6) − x²/2 − x³/2.

examples.title: A limit from a series
examples.q: Use a series expansion to find the limit of (1 − cos 2x)/x² as x → 0.

fills.q: The first two terms of sin x.

exam.stem: f(x) = ln(1 + sin x), for −π/2 < x < π/2.

parts.q: Show that f″(x) = −1/(1 + sin x).
ms: f′(x) = cos x/(1 + sin x) and applies the quotient rule
uses sin²x + cos²x = 1 in the numerator: −(1 + sin x)

parts.q: Find the Maclaurin series for f(x) up to and including the term in x³.
Write down the series expansion of e^(−2x) up to and including the term in x³.
ms: replaces x by −2x in the series for eˣ

parts.q: Hence find the series expansion of (1 + 3x)e^(−2x) up to and including the term in x³.
ms: multiplies and collects terms up to x³

parts.q: Use the first three non-zero terms of the series for cos x to estimate ∫ cos(x²) dx from 0 to 0.5, giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
ms: replaces x by x² in the cosine series
integrates term by term: x − x⁵/10 + x⁹/216

lessons.title: Improper integrals and volumes of revolution
notes: An improper integral has an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand at a boundary. Replace the problematic endpoint by a variable and take a one-sided limit after integrating. Writing infinity directly into an antiderivative is not a justification of convergence.

A solid formed by rotating y = f(x) about the x-axis has volume π∫y² dx over the specified interval. Rotation about the y-axis can use π∫x² dy. The squared radius and the integration variable must match the slices.

example.q: Evaluate the integral from 1 to infinity of 1/x² dx.
steps: Use a finite upper limit R.
The integral from 1 to R is [−1/x] = 1 − 1/R.
As R tends to infinity, 1/R tends to zero.

practice.q: The curve y = √x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume.
steps: State cubic units if x and y are measured in a length unit.

check.q: Evaluate the convergent integral from 1 to infinity of x⁻².

deep.tip: Name what makes the integral improper, an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand, and replace that limit by a letter before integrating. Convergence is decided by the limit of the evaluated expression, so write that limit step explicitly; for volumes, square the function first and keep π outside.

examples.title: An unbounded integrand
examples.q: Evaluate ∫ x^(−1/2) dx from 0 to 1.
steps: The integrand is unbounded at x = 0, so use the lower limit a and let a → 0⁺.

examples.title: An infinite limit with integration by parts
examples.q: Evaluate ∫ xe^(−x) dx from 0 to ∞.
steps: By parts with u = x, dv/dx = e^(−x): ∫ xe^(−x) dx = −xe^(−x) − e^(−x).

examples.title: Rotation about the y-axis
examples.q: The region bounded by y = x², the y-axis and y = 4 (x ≥ 0) is rotated through 2π about the y-axis. Find the volume.
steps: About the y-axis, V = π∫ x² dy.
Here x² = y, so V = π∫ y dy from 0 to 4.

parts.q: Show that ∫ 1/[x(x + 1)] dx from 1 to ∞ converges and find its exact value.
ms: considers the limit as the upper limit t → ∞

exam.stem: The region R lies under the curve y = 1/x for x ≥ 1 and above the x-axis.

parts.q: Show that the area of R is not finite.
ms: ∫ 1/x dx from 1 to t = ln t
ln t → ∞ as t → ∞, so the integral diverges

parts.q: R is rotated through 2π about the x-axis. Show that the volume generated is finite and find it.
ms: π∫ x⁻² dx from 1 to t

parts.q: Find the mean value of sin²x over the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ π.
The curve y = e^(−x), 0 ≤ x ≤ ln 2, is rotated through 2π about the x-axis. Find the exact volume generated.

lessons.title: Inverse trigonometric calculus and substitutions
notes: Differentiate inverse sine by implicit differentiation, respecting its principal range. The standard forms ∫1/√(a²−x²) dx and ∫1/(a²+x²) dx lead to inverse trigonometric functions with scale factors. A substitution must transform dx as well as the integrand.

For x = a sinθ, choose a range for θ that makes the square root sign consistent. Other algebraic and trigonometric substitutions can simplify roots or rational functions. Differentiate your antiderivative to check the constant factors.

example.q: Evaluate ∫1/(9 + x²) dx.
steps: This simplifies to 1/(9+x²), confirming the scale.

practice.q: Find ∫1/√(16 − x²) dx and state an appropriate real domain.
steps: Use a = 4 in the inverse-sine form.
It applies on an interval inside −4 < x < 4.

check.q: What is the coefficient multiplying arctan(x/3) in ∫dx/(9+x²)?

deep.tip: Match the integrand to a standard form before anything else: a² + x² leads to arctan, √(a² − x²) to arcsin. Complete the square to create that form, take any constant factor out so the coefficient of x² is 1, and check the answer by differentiating.

examples.title: Differentiating an inverse sine
examples.q: Differentiate arcsin 2x with respect to x.
steps: Let y = arcsin 2x, so sin y = 2x.
cos y = √(1 − sin²y) = √(1 − 4x²), positive because −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2.

examples.title: Completing the square
examples.q: Find ∫ 1/(x² + 4x + 13) dx.
steps: This is 1/(u² + a²) with u = x + 2 and a = 3.

examples.title: A definite inverse-sine integral
examples.q: Evaluate ∫ 1/√(4 − x²) dx from 0 to 1.

fills.q: Gradient of y = arctan x at x = 1.

parts.q: Show that d/dx(arctan x) = 1/(1 + x²).
ms: tan y = x, so sec²y dy/dx = 1

parts.q: Find the gradient of the curve y = arctan 3x at the point where x = ⅓.
Find the exact value of ∫ 1/√(9 − 4x²) dx from 0 to ¾.
ms: substitutes the limits: ½ arcsin ½

parts.q: Find ∫ (2x + 3)/(x² + 9) dx.
Hence find the exact value of the integral from 0 to 3.

lessons.title: Vector lines, scalar products and angles
notes: A line has vector equation r = a + λd, where a locates a point and d is a non-zero direction vector. Intersections require all three coordinates to agree for the same parameter pair. In 3D, non-parallel lines can be skew rather than intersecting.

The scalar product a·b = |a||b|cosθ gives angles and perpendicularity. For the acute angle between unoriented lines use the absolute value of the dot product. A shortest point-to-line distance can be found by locating the perpendicular foot and solving the scalar-product condition.

example.q: Find the angle between direction vectors (1,1,0) and (1,0,1).

practice.q: Find where r = (1,0,2) + λ(1,2,−1) intersects the plane x + y + z = 6.

check.q: Find the scalar product (1,1,0)·(1,0,1).

deep.tip: Use different parameters for different lines and solve two component equations before testing the third: that test is what separates intersecting from skew lines. Angles between lines come from direction vectors only, and the shortest distance from a point to a line uses a perpendicular, found with a zero scalar product.

examples.title: Do two lines meet?
examples.q: l₁: r = (1,2,3) + λ(1,−1,2) and l₂: r = (4,1,6) + μ(1,1,−1). Show that the lines intersect and find the point of intersection.
steps: z: 3 + 2λ = 7 and 6 − μ = 7, so the third equation is satisfied.

examples.title: Angle between two lines
examples.q: Find the acute angle between the lines in the previous example.
steps: Use the directions a = (1,−1,2) and b = (1,1,−1).
cos θ = |−2|/(√6 √3) = 2/√18, taking the modulus for the acute angle.

examples.title: Distance from a point to a line
examples.q: Find the shortest distance from P(3,1,2) to the line r = (1,0,−1) + t(2,1,2).
steps: The foot of the perpendicular has t = AP·d/|d|² = 11/9.

parts.q: Show that l₁ and l₂ intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection.
Find the acute angle between l₁ and l₂, to 1 decimal place.

exam.stem: A has coordinates (1, 2, −1) and B has coordinates (3, 0, 3).

parts.q: Find a vector equation of the line AB.
Find the coordinates of the point P on AB that is closest to the origin, and the distance OP.
Show that l₁ and l₂ are skew.
ms: equates components: 1 + λ = 0, λ = 1 + μ, 0 = 3 + μ
solves two of them: λ = −1, μ = −2
the third gives μ = −3, a contradiction
directions are not parallel, so the lines are skew

lessons.title: Planes, intersections and distances
notes: A plane with normal n through a satisfies (r−a)·n = 0. In Cartesian form ax+by+cz=d, the vector (a,b,c) is normal to the plane. The angle between planes is obtained from their normals; the acute line–plane angle is complementary to the acute line–normal angle.

The perpendicular distance from (x₀,y₀,z₀) to ax+by+cz=d is |ax₀+by₀+cz₀−d|/√(a²+b²+c²). For intersections, substitute a line into a plane or solve two plane equations with a free parameter. Check whether parallel objects are coincident before describing a distance.

example.q: Find the distance from (1,2,3) to 2x − y + 2z = 3.

practice.q: Find a Cartesian equation of the plane through (1,0,2) with normal (2,3,−1).
steps: The given point satisfies the equation.
The coefficient vector matches the specified normal.

check.q: Find the magnitude of the normal (2,−1,2).

deep.tip: Identify the normal vector first, because it controls every plane calculation: the equation r·n = a·n, the angle with a line (90° minus the angle with the normal) and the perpendicular distance. Substituting a line into a plane gives one linear equation in the parameter, so interpret the outcome: one value, none or all.

examples.title: A plane through three points
examples.q: Find a Cartesian equation of the plane through A(1,0,1), B(2,1,0) and C(0,2,3).
steps: A normal n = (a,b,c) satisfies a + b − c = 0 and −a + 2b + 2c = 0.
Adding: 3b + c = 0; taking b = −1 gives c = 3 and a = 4, so n = (4,−1,3).

examples.title: Angle between a line and a plane
examples.q: Find the angle between the line with direction (1,2,2) and the plane 2x − y + 2z = 5.
steps: The normal to the plane is n = (2,−1,2).
The angle φ between the line and the normal has cos φ = |2 − 2 + 4|/(3 × 3) = 4/9.
The angle between the line and the plane is θ = 90° − φ, so sin θ = 4/9.

examples.title: Line of intersection of two planes
examples.q: Find a vector equation of the line in which x + y + z = 3 and x − y + 2z = 2 meet.
steps: A direction d is perpendicular to both normals: d·(1,1,1) = 0 and d·(1,−1,2) = 0.
A common point: put z = 0, then x + y = 3 and x − y = 2, so x = 5/2, y = 1/2.

fills.q: The point (1, 2, 3) lies on x + y + z = d.

exam.stem: The plane Π has equation 2x − y + 2z = 5 and the line l has equation r = (1,3,−2) + λ(2,1,1).

parts.q: Find the coordinates of the point where l meets Π.
Find the acute angle between l and Π, to 1 decimal place.
ms: scalar product of (2,1,1) with the normal (2,−1,2): 5

parts.q: Find the perpendicular distance from the point (1, 3, −2) to Π.
Find the acute angle between the planes x + 2y − 2z = 5 and 2x − y + 2z = 1, to 1 decimal place.

exam.stem: The plane Π passes through A(2, 1, −1) and is perpendicular to the vector (1,−2,3).

parts.q: Find a Cartesian equation of Π.
Find the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular from Q(4, −3, 5) to Π.
ms: line through Q along the normal: (4 + t, −3 − 2t, 5 + 3t)

lessons.title: Polar curves, tangents and enclosed area
notes: Polar coordinates use x=r cosθ and y=r sinθ. A sketch should consider symmetry, zeros of r and the interval over which a loop is traced once. Negative r places a point on the opposite ray, so it must be interpreted rather than silently discarded.

The polar area is ½∫r² dθ. Check the bounds carefully to avoid counting a loop twice. For tangents, differentiate x(θ) and y(θ), then use dy/dx=(dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ); horizontal and vertical tangent tests must also consider points where both derivatives vanish.

example.q: Find the area of the circle r = 2cosθ, using −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.
steps: The interval traces the circle once.
This agrees with a circle of radius 1 centred at (1,0).

practice.q: Convert r = 4sinθ to Cartesian form and identify the curve.
steps: It is a circle with centre (0,2) and radius 2.

check.q: For r=4sinθ, what is the circle radius in Cartesian coordinates?

deep.tip: Sketch the curve from a short table of θ and r before integrating, so that the limits describe the region once and only once. Area uses ½∫r² dθ, tangents parallel to the initial line come from d(r sin θ)/dθ = 0, and tangents perpendicular to it from d(r cos θ)/dθ = 0.

examples.title: Area of a cardioid
examples.q: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos θ).
steps: Area = ½∫ r² dθ from 0 to 2π = 2∫ (1 + 2cos θ + cos²θ) dθ.
cos²θ = ½(1 + cos 2θ), so the integrand is 3/2 + 2cos θ + ½cos 2θ.
Over a full turn the cosine terms integrate to 0.

examples.title: Tangents parallel to the initial line
examples.q: Find the points on r = 1 + cos θ where the tangent is parallel to the initial line.
steps: y = r sin θ = sin θ + sin θ cos θ.
dy/dθ = cos θ + cos 2θ = 2cos²θ + cos θ − 1.
(2cos θ − 1)(cos θ + 1) = 0, so cos θ = ½ or cos θ = −1.
θ = ±π/3, where r = 3/2; θ = π is the pole, where the curve has a cusp.

examples.title: Where two curves meet
examples.q: Find the polar coordinates of the points where r = 1 + cos θ meets r = 3cos θ.
steps: The curves meet at (3/2, π/3) and (3/2, −π/3); both also pass through the pole, for different values of θ.

fills.q: The circle r = 2 in Cartesian form.
Area inside r = 3 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.
The circle r = 4cos θ at θ = π/3.

exam.stem: The curve C has polar equation r = 3 + 2cos θ, 0 ≤ θ < 2π.

parts.q: State the greatest and least values of r and the values of θ at which they occur.
Find the exact area enclosed by C.

exam.stem: The curve C has polar equation r = 2sin 2θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.

parts.q: Find the exact area enclosed by this loop of C.
State the greatest value of r on the loop and the value of θ at which it occurs.
Find the polar coordinates of the points on the curve r = 2(1 + cos θ), −π < θ ≤ π, at which the tangent is perpendicular to the initial line.
ms: (1, 2π/3) and (1, −2π/3); θ = π is the cusp at the pole

lessons.title: Hyperbolic functions, identities and inverses
notes: Define sinh x=(eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x=(eˣ+e⁻ˣ)/2. Their identity is cosh²x−sinh²x=1, with a minus sign. Differentiation gives d(sinh x)/dx=cosh x and d(cosh x)/dx=sinh x; use the chain rule for a scaled argument.

The inverse of cosh requires a domain restriction, commonly x≥0. Logarithmic inverse forms follow by solving an exponential equation. For arcosh x the real domain is x≥1; for artanh x it is |x|<1. Keep the required real domain when simplifying logarithms.

example.q: Solve cosh x = 5/3 for real x.
steps: x=ln3 or −ln3, consistent with cosh being even.

practice.q: Differentiate sinh(3x) and integrate cosh(2x).
steps: Differentiating the proposed integral restores cosh(2x).

check.q: Evaluate cosh(0).

deep.tip: Most equations become a quadratic in eˣ once the definitions are substituted, so multiply through by eˣ and reject any non-positive value of eˣ. Remember that cosh is even, so cosh x = k gives two solutions when k > 1, and that the identities differ from the trigonometric ones by the sign attached to sinh².

examples.title: An equation in sinh and cosh
examples.q: Solve 2cosh x − sinh x = 2.

examples.title: Proving an identity
examples.q: Prove that cosh²x − sinh²x = 1.

examples.title: An inverse hyperbolic value
examples.q: Find the exact value of arsinh(¾).

parts.q: Using the definitions in terms of exponentials, prove that sinh 2x = 2sinh x cosh x.
Hence solve sinh 2x = 3sinh x, giving non-zero answers as exact logarithms.
ms: cosh x = 3/2 and uses arcosh x = ln(x + √(x² − 1))

parts.q: Solve 5cosh x + 3sinh x = 4, giving your answer as an exact logarithm.
Show that d/dx(arsinh x) = 1/√(1 + x²).
ms: sinh y = x, so cosh y dy/dx = 1

parts.q: Hence find the exact value of ∫ 1/√(1 + x²) dx from 0 to ¾.

lessons.title: First-order differential equations and modelling
notes: A linear first-order equation y′+P(x)y=Q(x) has integrating factor exp(∫P dx). Multiplying every term makes the left side a product derivative. Apply an initial condition only after finding the general solution and keep the independent variable consistent.

In a model, identify what the variables and rate constants mean and whether the limiting behaviour is sensible. An initial value selects a particular solution; it does not prove that the model remains accurate indefinitely. A separable equation is a special convenient case, not the only first-order form.

example.q: Solve y′ + 2y = 6, given y(0)=1.
steps: The initial condition gives C=−2, so y=3−2e^(−2x).

practice.q: Solve y′ + y = 4 with y(0)=2.
steps: Multiply by the integrating factor eˣ.
The solution approaches 4 as x increases.

check.q: What is the equilibrium solution of y′+2y=6?

deep.tip: Rearrange to dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) with coefficient 1 on dy/dx before finding the integrating factor e^(∫P dx). Recognise the left side as the derivative of (integrating factor × y), integrate once with a constant, and apply the boundary condition only after that constant is in place.

examples.title: Integrating factor with a power of x
examples.q: Find the general solution of dy/dx + y/x = x², x > 0.
steps: P = 1/x, so the integrating factor is e^(ln x) = x.
x dy/dx + y = x³, that is d(xy)/dx = x³.

examples.title: Integrating factor with an exponential
examples.q: Find the general solution of dy/dx − 2y = e^(3x).

examples.title: A mixing model
examples.q: A tank holds 100 litres of water. Brine containing 2 g of salt per litre flows in at 3 litres per minute and the mixture flows out at the same rate. Initially there is no salt. Find the mass m grams of salt after t minutes.
steps: Rate in = 6 g/min; rate out = 3 × m/100 g/min, so dm/dt = 6 − 0.03m.
m = 200(1 − e^(−0.03t)); the mass approaches 200 g.

exam.stem: dy/dx + 2y/x = 4x, x > 0.

parts.q: Find the general solution of the differential equation.
Given that y = 3 when x = 1, find the value of y when x = 2.

exam.stem: dy/dx + y tan x = cos x, with y = 2 when x = 0.

parts.q: Find y in terms of x and hence the value of y when x = π.

exam.stem: A particle falls from rest. Its speed v m s⁻¹ after t seconds satisfies dv/dt = 9.8 − 0.2v.

parts.q: Find v in terms of t.
State the terminal speed.
Find the time taken to reach half the terminal speed, to 3 significant figures.

lessons.title: Second-order equations and complementary functions
notes: For ay″+by′+cy=0, solve the auxiliary equation ar²+br+c=0, obtained by trying y=e^(rx). Distinct real roots give a sum of exponentials; a repeated root requires (A+Bx)e^(rx). Complex roots α±iβ give e^(αx)(Acosβx+Bsinβx).

For a non-zero forcing term, add a particular integral to the complementary function. If a trial form duplicates a term of the complementary function, multiply it by a sufficient power of x. Verify by substitution before applying the two initial or boundary conditions.

example.q: Solve y″−3y′+2y=0 with y(0)=0 and y′(0)=1.

practice.q: Find the general solution of y″+4y=8.
steps: Try a constant particular integral K; 4K=8 gives K=2.

check.q: For y″−3y′+2y=0, what is the larger auxiliary root?

deep.tip: Solve the auxiliary equation and classify its roots before writing anything else: two real roots, a repeated root and complex roots each have their own form of complementary function. Choose a particular integral that matches the right-hand side, and apply initial conditions only to the full general solution.

examples.title: A repeated root
examples.q: Solve y″ + 4y′ + 4y = 0 given that y = 1 and y′ = 0 when x = 0.
steps: Auxiliary equation m² + 4m + 4 = 0 has the repeated root m = −2.

examples.title: Complex roots
examples.q: Find the general solution of y″ + 2y′ + 5y = 0.
steps: The real part gives the exponential factor and the imaginary part the frequency.

examples.title: A polynomial particular integral
examples.q: Find the general solution of y″ − 3y′ + 2y = 4x.
steps: m² − 3m + 2 = 0 gives m = 1, 2, so the complementary function is Aeˣ + Be^(2x).
Try y = ax + b: then y′ = a and y″ = 0.

parts.q: Find the complementary function.
Find a particular integral.
Given that y = 3 and y′ = 6 when x = 0, find y in terms of x.
Find the general solution.
Describe the behaviour of y as x → ∞.
ms: oscillations whose amplitude decays to zero

parts.q: Solve y″ + 4y = 12sin x, given that y = 0 and y′ = 6 when x = 0.
ms: particular integral of the form λ sin x + μ cos x
applies both conditions to the general solution

lessons.title: Coupled equations and physical interpretations
notes: Differentiate one of a pair of first-order linear equations and eliminate the other dependent variable to obtain a second-order equation. Solve it and use the original first-order relation to recover the second variable. The initial conditions for a derivative may come from the other variable.

Interpret damping and forcing through the roots and particular integral. A negative real part in the complementary function corresponds to decay; purely imaginary roots give undamped oscillation. Boundary values and units should support the model, and any small-angle or proportional-resistance assumption must be stated.

example.q: Solve x′=y and y′=−4x with x(0)=1 and y(0)=0.
steps: y(0)=0 gives B=0; x=cos2t and y=−2sin2t.

practice.q: For x′=y and y′=−9x, find x and y when x(0)=0 and y(0)=3.
steps: x(0)=0 gives A=0; y(0)=3B=3 gives B=1.
Both original equations and both initial values are satisfied.

check.q: For x″=−9x, what is the positive angular frequency?

deep.tip: For a coupled pair, differentiate one equation and use the other to eliminate one variable, giving a single second-order equation; then recover the second variable from the original first-order equation rather than solving again. In a damped model, compare the discriminant of the auxiliary equation with zero to name the type of damping.

examples.title: Eliminating one variable
examples.q: Solve dx/dt = 3x − y and dy/dt = 2x for x and y in terms of t.
steps: Differentiate the first equation: x″ = 3x′ − y′ = 3x′ − 2x.
From the first equation y = 3x − x′.

examples.title: Simple harmonic motion
examples.q: A particle moves so that x″ = −9x, with x = 2 and x′ = 0 when t = 0. Find x, the period and the maximum speed.
steps: x″ + 9x = 0 gives x = A cos 3t + B sin 3t.
x(0) = 2 gives A = 2 and x′(0) = 0 gives B = 0.
x′ = −6sin 3t, so the maximum speed is 6.

examples.title: Classifying damping
examples.q: Classify the damping in x″ + 6x′ + 9x = 0 and in x″ + 2x′ + 9x = 0.
steps: A repeated root: critical damping, x = (A + Bt)e^(−3t), with no oscillation.
Complex roots −1 ± 2√2 i: light damping, oscillations with decaying amplitude.

exam.stem: dx/dt = 4x − 2y and dy/dt = x + y, with x = 3 and y = 2 when t = 0.

parts.q: Show that d²x/dt² − 5 dx/dt + 6x = 0.
Find x and y in terms of t.

exam.stem: The displacement x of a damped oscillator satisfies x″ + 4x′ + 13x = 0, with x = 0 and x′ = 6 when t = 0.

parts.q: Find x in terms of t.
ms: applies both initial conditions to e^(−2t)(A cos 3t + B sin 3t)

parts.q: State the type of damping.
Find the first time after t = 0 at which x = 0.

exam.stem: A particle moves on a line so that x″ = −4x, with x = 3 and x′ = 8 when t = 0.

parts.q: Find x in terms of t and the amplitude of the motion.
Find the maximum speed.

lessons.title: Half-angle substitutions and trigonometric equations
notes: With t=tan(θ/2), sinθ=2t/(1+t²), cosθ=(1−t²)/(1+t²) and tanθ=2t/(1−t²). These rational forms turn many trigonometric equations into polynomial equations in t. Derive them from double-angle identities rather than treating t as tanθ.

The substitution misses angles at which tan(θ/2) is undefined. Test those angles in the original equation. Map every t-root back into the stated θ-interval, and reject values introduced by multiplying a denominator that can be zero.

example.q: Solve sinθ=cosθ for 0≤θ<2π using t=tan(θ/2).
steps: Converting to θ gives π/4 and 5π/4.
The missing substitution point θ=π is not a solution.

practice.q: Use the t-formulae to solve sinθ=1−cosθ for 0≤θ<2π.
steps: t=0 gives θ=0; t=1 gives θ=π/2.
The two solutions are 0 and π/2.

check.q: If t=tan(θ/2)=1, what is sinθ?

deep.tip: Substitute for every trigonometric function at once and multiply through by 1 + t² straight away, so the equation becomes a polynomial in t. The substitution cannot represent θ = π (where t is undefined), so test that value separately, and convert each t back with θ = 2arctan t, adjusting into the required interval.

examples.title: A repeated root in t
examples.q: Solve 3cos θ + 4sin θ = 5 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π, using t = tan(θ/2).
steps: θ = 2arctan ½ = 0.927 (3 s.f.); θ = π gives −3 ≠ 5, so nothing is lost.

examples.title: Proving an identity
examples.q: Use t = tan(θ/2) to prove that (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = tan(θ/2).
steps: So (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = tan(θ/2), for sin θ ≠ 0.

exam.stem: The equation sin θ + 2cos θ = 1 is to be solved for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.

parts.q: Using t = tan(θ/2), show that 3t² − 2t − 1 = 0.
Hence solve the equation, giving answers to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
Use t = tan(θ/2) to prove that sin θ/(1 + cos θ) = tan(θ/2).
Show that sec θ + tan θ = (1 + t)/(1 − t), where t = tan(θ/2).
Hence solve sec θ + tan θ = 3 for 0 < θ < π/2.

lessons.title: Taylor expansions about a non-zero point
notes: Taylor expansion about x=a uses h=x−a and derivatives evaluated at a. The expansion is f(a)+hf′(a)+h²f″(a)/2!+… . Retain enough terms before dividing by a power of h or taking a limit, and identify any interval required for convergence.

A numerical approximation should state the expansion point, retained order and why the input is close to that point. A truncated series is not an equality valid for every x. The leading neglected term can give a useful indication of error, but is not automatically a rigorous error bound.

example.q: Expand ln x about x=1 through (x−1)³.
steps: The power series converges for |h|<1; endpoints require separate checks.

practice.q: Find the quadratic Taylor approximation to √x about x=4.
steps: Use the approximation close to x=4 and distinguish it from an exact identity.

check.q: What is the coefficient of (x−1)² in the Taylor expansion of ln x about 1?

deep.tip: Set h = x − a and tabulate f(a), f′(a), f″(a), … before writing the series, remembering the factorial under each derivative. A Taylor polynomial is only reliable near x = a, so choose the centre closest to the value you want and say how far from it you are.

examples.title: Expanding about π/6
examples.q: Find the Taylor series of sin x in ascending powers of (x − π/6) up to the term in (x − π/6)².
steps: f(x) = sin x, f′(x) = cos x, f″(x) = −sin x.
f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)h + f″(a)h²/2 with h = x − π/6.

examples.title: An exponential about x = 1
examples.q: Find the Taylor series of eˣ about x = 1 up to the term in (x − 1)³.
steps: Every derivative of eˣ is eˣ, so each equals e at x = 1.

exam.stem: f(x) = tan x.

parts.q: Show that f″(x) = 2sec²x tan x.
ms: f′(x) = sec²x and uses the chain rule
2sec x × sec x tan x = 2sec²x tan x

parts.q: Find the Taylor series of tan x in ascending powers of (x − π/4) up to the term in (x − π/4)².
Use your series to estimate tan 0.8, to 4 decimal places.
Find the Taylor series of 1/x about x = 2 up to and including the term in (x − 2)³.
Find the Taylor series of ln x about x = e up to and including the term in (x − e)².

lessons.title: Leibniz differentiation and indeterminate limits
notes: Leibniz’s theorem gives the nth derivative of a product as a binomial sum of derivatives of its factors. When one factor is a low-degree polynomial, most terms vanish. Check the derivative orders and binomial coefficients explicitly.

L’Hospital’s rule applies to suitable 0/0 or infinity/infinity limits when its hypotheses are met. Differentiate numerator and denominator separately, not the quotient as one function. Recheck the indeterminate form before applying the rule again; it is not a replacement for ordinary substitution in a determinate limit.

example.q: Find the nth derivative of x eˣ and evaluate the limit of (eˣ−1−x)/x² as x→0.
steps: Only the zeroth and first derivatives of x are non-zero.
The limit is 0/0; apply L’Hospital to obtain (eˣ−1)/(2x).
It remains 0/0; apply the rule again to obtain eˣ/2.

practice.q: Find the nth derivative of x²eˣ.
steps: The surviving derivatives of x² are x², 2x and 2.
The expression also works for n=0 and n=1.

check.q: Evaluate the limit of (eˣ−1−x)/x² as x tends to 0.

deep.tip: For a product, let u be the factor whose derivatives vanish after a few steps, so the Leibniz sum stops early; write the binomial coefficients first. Before using L’Hôpital’s rule, confirm that the limit really has the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, and re-check that form each time you apply the rule again.

examples.title: Leibniz’s theorem
examples.q: Find the fourth derivative of x² sin x.
steps: Take u = x² (derivatives 2x, 2, 0) and v = sin x.
Fourth derivative = u v⁗ + 4u′v‴ + 6u″v″, the later terms being zero.
= x² sin x − 8x cos x − 12 sin x.

examples.title: L’Hôpital’s rule used three times
examples.q: Find the limit of (sin x − x)/x³ as x → 0.
steps: The form is 0/0: differentiate top and bottom to get (cos x − 1)/3x².
Still 0/0: differentiate again to get −sin x/6x.
Still 0/0: differentiate again to get −cos x/6.

fills.q: A binomial coefficient in Leibniz’s theorem.

lines: the limit of sin 3x / x as x → 0 is [[3]]

fills.q: The third derivative of e^(2x) at x = 0.

parts.q: Use Leibniz’s theorem to find the fifth derivative of x³e^(2x).
ms: Leibniz with u = x³, v = e^(2x), terms r = 0 to 3
uses 3x², 6x, 6 and powers of 2 from e^(2x)

parts.q: Find the limit of (e^(2x) − 1 − 2x)/x² as x → 0.
Find the limit of [x − ln(1 + x)]/(1 − cos x) as x → 0.
ms: applies the rule again: (1 + x)⁻²/cos x

parts.q: Find the limit of (1 − sin x)/cos²x as x → π/2.
ms: form 0/0; differentiates: −cos x/(−2cos x sin x)

lessons.title: Weierstrass substitution in integration
notes: The substitution t=tan(x/2) makes sine and cosine rational: sin x=2t/(1+t²), cos x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), and dx=2dt/(1+t²). Transform the differential as well as the integrand and apply ordinary rational integration.

The substitution is local to an interval avoiding its singular points. An antiderivative may have different equivalent inverse-trigonometric forms on different intervals. For a definite integral, transform the limits carefully and check whether the interval crosses a substitution discontinuity.

example.q: Find ∫dx/(2+cos x) using t=tan(x/2).
steps: Replace t by tan(x/2), on an interval where the substitution is valid.

practice.q: Use the same substitution to find ∫dx/(3+2cos x).
steps: State that a suitable continuous branch is used.

check.q: For t=tan(x/2), what is dt/dx at x=0?

deep.tip: Replace dx as well as the trigonometric functions: dx = 2dt/(1 + t²). The factor 1 + t² usually cancels, leaving a rational function of t. Change the limits to values of t, or substitute back, and keep to an interval of x on which tan(x/2) is continuous.

examples.title: A denominator that becomes a perfect square
examples.q: Find ∫ 1/(1 + sin x) dx using t = tan(x/2).
steps: dx = 2dt/(1 + t²), so the integral is ∫ 2/(1 + t)² dt.

examples.title: A definite integral with new limits
examples.q: Evaluate ∫ 1/(5 + 4cos x) dx from 0 to π/2.
steps: Limits: x = 0 gives t = 0 and x = π/2 gives t = 1.
[⅔ arctan(t/3)] from 0 to 1 = ⅔ arctan ⅓ ≈ 0.2145.

parts.q: Using t = tan(x/2), show that ∫ 1/(1 + sin x + cos x) dx = ∫ 1/(1 + t) dt.
ms: substitutes for sin x, cos x and dx

parts.q: Hence find the exact value of the integral from 0 to π/2.
Use the substitution t = tan(x/2) to find the exact value of ∫ 1/(2 − cos x) dx from 0 to π/2.
ms: substitutes for cos x and dx

parts.q: Use the substitution t = tan(x/2) to show that ∫ cosec x dx = ln|tan(x/2)| + c.
ms: cosec x = (1 + t²)/2t and dx = 2dt/(1 + t²)

lessons.title: Taylor methods and substitutions for differential equations
notes: Successive derivatives of a differential equation can produce a local Taylor solution from initial data. Calculate each derivative from the original relation before evaluating it at the starting point. A transformed dependent variable can also make a non-linear-looking equation separable or linear.

The resulting finite polynomial is an approximation near the initial point, not the complete exact solution. In an exact substitution, recover the original dependent variable and apply its original initial condition. Always test whether a substitution introduces restrictions or excludes a constant solution.

example.q: For y′=x+y and y(0)=1, find the cubic Taylor approximation at zero.

practice.q: For y′=y² and y(0)=1, find the cubic Taylor polynomial.
steps: It agrees locally with the exact solution 1/(1−x).

check.q: For y′=x+y and y(0)=1, find y″(0).

deep.tip: For a series solution, differentiate the differential equation itself to obtain each higher derivative, and evaluate at the initial point after every differentiation. For a substitution, differentiate the substitution first, replace dy/dx completely, and only then solve; return to the original variables at the end.

examples.title: A series solution of a second-order equation
examples.q: y″ = 2y′ − xy with y = 1 and y′ = 2 at x = 0. Find the series solution up to the term in x³.

examples.title: A substitution that separates the variables
examples.q: Use u = x + y to solve dy/dx = (x + y)².
steps: ∫ du/(1 + u²) = ∫ dx gives arctan u = x + c.

exam.stem: d²y/dx² + x dy/dx + y = 0, with y = 1 and dy/dx = 0 at x = 0.

parts.q: Find the value of d²y/dx² at x = 0.
Show that d³y/dx³ + x d²y/dx² + 2 dy/dx = 0.
ms: differentiates, using the product rule on x dy/dx

parts.q: Find the series solution for y up to and including the term in x⁴.
ms: uses the Taylor formula with 2! and 4!

exam.stem: dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), x > 0.

parts.q: Use the substitution y = ux to show that x du/dx = 1/u.
Given that y = 2 when x = 1, find y² in terms of x.

exam.stem: dy/dx = x² − y², with y = 1 at x = 0.

parts.q: Find a series solution for y up to and including the term in x³.
Use your series to estimate y when x = 0.1, to 4 decimal places.

lessons.title: Conics, eccentricity, tangents and loci
notes: Parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas can be described by focus–directrix relationships. For x²/a²+y²/b²=1 with a>b>0, the foci are (±ae,0), e²=1−b²/a² and the directrices are x=±a/e. A hyperbola instead has e²=1+b²/a².

Use implicit or parametric differentiation to obtain a tangent. At a point on an ellipse, the tangent is xx₁/a²+yy₁/b²=1. Check that the point lies on the curve before using a tangent formula. A parabola y²=4ax has focus (a,0) and directrix x=−a.

example.q: For x²/25+y²/9=1, find the eccentricity, foci and tangent at (3,12/5).

practice.q: For y²=12x, find the focus, directrix and tangent at (3,6).
steps: Differentiate: 2y y′=12, so at the point the gradient is 1.
The tangent is y−6=x−3, or y=x+3.

check.q: For x²/25+y²/9=1, find the positive x-coordinate of a focus.

deep.tip: Identify the conic and its parameters (a, b, e or the focal length) before any calculus. Parametric points such as (at², 2at), (a cos θ, b sin θ) and (ct, c/t) make gradients short: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). For a locus, eliminate the parameter at the very end.

examples.title: A hyperbola and its features
examples.q: For the hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1, find the eccentricity, the foci, the directrices and the asymptotes.
steps: a = 4, b = 3 and b² = a²(e² − 1), so e² = 1 + 9/16.

examples.title: Tangent and normal to a parabola
examples.q: The point P on y² = 8x has parameter t = 3. Find the tangent and the normal at P.
steps: Tangent: y − 12 = ⅓(x − 18), that is 3y = x + 18.
Normal has gradient −3: y − 12 = −3(x − 18), that is y + 3x = 66.

examples.title: Tangent to a rectangular hyperbola
examples.q: Find the equation of the tangent to xy = 16 at the point (4t, 4/t).

parts.q: Find the eccentricity of E.
Write down the coordinates of the foci and the equations of the directrices.
Show that the tangent to E at P(3cos θ, 2sin θ) has equation 2x cos θ + 3y sin θ = 6.
ms: uses cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 to reach the given equation

exam.stem: The point P(t², 2t) lies on the parabola y² = 4x.

parts.q: Show that the normal at P has equation y + tx = 2t + t³.
The normal at the point where t = 1 meets the parabola again at Q. Find the coordinates of Q.

exam.stem: The point P(4p, 4/p), p > 0, lies on the rectangular hyperbola xy = 16. The tangent at P meets the axes at A and B.

parts.q: Show that the area of triangle OAB is the same for every position of P.

lessons.title: Vector products, areas and triple products
notes: The vector product a×b is perpendicular to both vectors; its magnitude is the area of their parallelogram. Its order matters because b×a=−a×b. Use components with a consistent cofactor-sign pattern and check that the result has zero scalar product with each original vector.

The absolute scalar triple product |a·(b×c)| is a parallelepiped volume; divide by 6 for the tetrahedron formed by the three edges from a common vertex. A zero triple product indicates coplanarity, provided the geometrical interpretation uses the correct common origin.

example.q: For a=(1,0,1), b=(0,2,0), find a×b and the triangle area.
steps: The triangle area is half the parallelogram area: √2.
Both a·(a×b) and b·(a×b) equal zero.

practice.q: Find the volume of the tetrahedron with edge vectors (2,0,0), (0,3,0), (0,0,4) from the same vertex.
steps: The scalar triple product has magnitude 2×3×4=24.
A tetrahedron occupies one sixth of that parallelepiped.

check.q: Find the volume of a parallelepiped with perpendicular edge lengths 2,3,4.

deep.tip: Set the vector product out as a determinant and check it with two scalar products, both of which must be zero. Its magnitude is the area of a parallelogram, so halve it for a triangle; the scalar triple product gives the volume of a parallelepiped, so divide by 6 for a tetrahedron.

examples.title: A vector product and an area
examples.q: a = (2,1,−1) and b = (1,3,2). Find a × b and the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b.

examples.title: A plane from three points
examples.q: Find a Cartesian equation of the plane through A(1,1,0), B(2,0,1) and C(0,2,3).
steps: A normal is (1, 1, 0), so the plane is x + y = d.
Using A: d = 2, so x + y = 2; B and C both satisfy this.

examples.title: A scalar triple product
examples.q: Find the volume of the parallelepiped with edges a = (1,2,0), b = (0,1,3) and c = (2,0,1).
steps: Volume = |a·(b × c)|, the determinant with rows a, b, c.

fills.q: |a| = 3, |b| = 4 and the angle between them is 30°.
A vector product is perpendicular to both factors.

parts.q: Find AB × AC.
Find the exact area of triangle ABC.
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane ABC.
ms: x − 5y − 3z = d with a point substituted

parts.q: The tetrahedron OABC has OA = (2,1,0), OB = (1,3,1) and OC = (0,1,4). Find its volume.
ms: scalar triple product as a 3 × 3 determinant

exam.stem: The line l passes through the point with position vector a = (1,2,−1) and has direction d = (2,1,2).

parts.q: Write down an equation of l in the form (r − a) × d = 0.
Find the shortest distance from the origin to l.

lessons.title: Simpson, numerical differential equations and inequalities
notes: Simpson’s rule uses an even number of equal subintervals and alternating weights 1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1. Its estimate is h/3 times the weighted sum. State the interval and spacing before inserting values. Euler and central-difference methods require equally careful indexing of the point or derivative being approximated.

For rational or modulus inequalities, locate zeros and excluded denominator values before testing sign intervals. Multiplying through by an expression of unknown sign is unsafe. A numerical approximation can suggest a solution, but algebra and sign checks establish the inequality intervals.

example.q: Use Simpson’s rule with 2 intervals to estimate ∫₀²x² dx, then solve (x−1)/(x+2)>0.
steps: The sign boundaries are x=−2 and x=1.
The quotient is positive when x<−2 or x>1.
Exclude −2 because the expression is undefined, and 1 because the inequality is strict.

practice.q: Use one Euler step of length 0.1 for y′=x+y from (0,1).
steps: This is a numerical estimate, not an exact solution.

check.q: How many subintervals are used when Simpson ordinates are y₀,y₁,y₂,y₃,y₄?

deep.tip: Tabulate ordinates to at least one more decimal place than the answer needs, and check that Simpson’s rule has an even number of strips. For an inequality, never multiply by an expression whose sign is unknown: collect everything on one side as a single fraction, find the critical values and test each region.

examples.title: Simpson’s rule with four strips
examples.q: Use Simpson’s rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ ln x dx from 1 to 3.

examples.title: A rational inequality
examples.q: Solve 2x/(x − 1) < 3.
steps: Critical values x = 1 and x = 3; test a value in each region.

examples.title: A two-step numerical solution
examples.q: dy/dx = x − y² with y = 1 at x = 0. Use h = 0.1 with y₁ ≈ y₀ + hf(x₀, y₀) and then y₂ ≈ y₀ + 2hf(x₁, y₁) to estimate y at x = 0.2.

fills.q: Simpson’s rule weights for four strips.
One Euler step for y′ = 2x + y from (0, 1) with h = 0.1.

parts.q: Use Simpson’s rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx from 0 to 1, giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
Hence obtain an estimate for π.

exam.stem: dy/dx = x² + y, with y = 1 at x = 0. Use a step length of 0.1.

parts.q: Use y₁ ≈ y₀ + h(dy/dx)₀ to estimate y at x = 0.1.
Use y₂ ≈ y₀ + 2h(dy/dx)₁ to estimate y at x = 0.2.
Solve |2x − 1| < x + 4.

lessons.title: Groups, subgroups, orders and isomorphisms
notes: A group has a closed associative operation, an identity and an inverse for every element. Commutativity is an additional property, not a group axiom. A Cayley table can establish closure, identity and inverses in a finite example, but associativity needs justification beyond a visual pattern.

The order of a finite group is its number of elements; an element’s order is the least positive power giving the identity. Lagrange’s theorem makes subgroup orders divide the group order, but divisibility alone does not prove a subset is a subgroup. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving the operation.

example.q: In the additive group of integers modulo 6, find the order of 2 and its generated subgroup.
steps: The subgroup order 3 divides the group order 6.

practice.q: Find the orders of 1 and 3 in the additive group modulo 8.
steps: For 3, 8×3=24≡0 modulo 8 and no smaller positive multiple is 0.

check.q: Find the order of 2 in the additive group modulo 6.

deep.tip: Check the four axioms in order: closure, associativity (often inherited from ordinary arithmetic or composition), identity and inverses. Lagrange’s theorem limits the possible orders of subgroups and elements to divisors of the group order; a group is cyclic exactly when some element has order equal to the group order.

examples.title: A multiplicative group modulo 8
examples.q: Show that G = {1, 3, 5, 7} under multiplication modulo 8 is a group, and find the order of each element.
steps: Multiplication modulo 8 is associative; the identity is 1.
Each element is its own inverse, since a² ≡ 1 for every a in G.
So G is a group; 1 has order 1 and 3, 5, 7 each have order 2.
No element has order 4, so G is not cyclic: it is isomorphic to the Klein four-group.

examples.title: Lagrange’s theorem
examples.q: In the group of integers modulo 12 under addition, find the order of 8 and the subgroup it generates, and list the possible orders of subgroups.
steps: By Lagrange’s theorem the order of any subgroup divides 12.

exam.stem: G = {1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8} under multiplication modulo 9.

parts.q: Show that 2 is a generator of G.
Find the order of 4.
Write down a subgroup of G of order 2.
State, with a reason, whether G is isomorphic to the integers modulo 6 under addition.
ms: both groups are cyclic of order 6

exam.stem: D₃ is the group of symmetries of an equilateral triangle under composition.

parts.q: State the possible orders of subgroups of D₃.
Explain why D₃ is not cyclic.
ms: the rotations have order 3 or 1 and the reflections order 2
no element has order 6, so no single element generates the group

parts.q: State, with a reason, whether D₃ is abelian.
ms: no: two different reflections composed in opposite orders give different rotations

exam.stem: The operation ∗ is defined on S = {x ∈ ℝ : x ≠ −1} by a ∗ b = a + b + ab.

parts.q: Show that a ∗ b = (1 + a)(1 + b) − 1, and hence show that S is closed under ∗.
Show that ∗ is associative.
ms: writes (a ∗ b) ∗ c using the product form
both bracketings equal (1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) − 1

parts.q: Find the identity element and the inverse of 3.

lessons.title: Reduction formulae, arc length and surface area
notes: Integration by parts can connect Iₙ to Iₙ₋₂ or another simpler member of a family. Keep boundary terms until they have been evaluated; a recurrence for definite integrals need not have the same boundary term as one for indefinite integrals.

Cartesian arc length is ∫√(1+y′²) dx. Surface area around the x-axis is 2π∫y√(1+y′²) dx when the radius is y≥0. Parametric and polar forms use the corresponding element of arc length. The radius factor distinguishes surface area from arc length.

example.q: Find the length of y=(2/3)x^(3/2) from x=0 to x=3.

practice.q: If Iₙ=∫₀^(π/2)sinⁿx dx and Iₙ=(n−1)Iₙ₋₂/n, calculate I₄.
steps: The given recurrence is used only for n≥2.

check.q: If I₀=π/2 and I₂=I₀/2, find I₂/π.

deep.tip: Integrate by parts so that the power drops, and write the result in terms of Iₙ₋₁ or Iₙ₋₂ before substituting any limits. Evaluate the boundary terms carefully, find the starting integral I₀ or I₁ directly, and step up one index at a time. For arc length and surface area, simplify 1 + (dy/dx)² before integrating; it is often a perfect square.

examples.title: A reduction formula with an exponential
examples.q: Iₙ = ∫ xⁿeˣ dx from 0 to 1. Show that Iₙ = e − nIₙ₋₁ and find I₃.
steps: By parts: Iₙ = [xⁿeˣ] from 0 to 1 − n∫ xⁿ⁻¹eˣ dx.
The boundary term is e − 0, so Iₙ = e − nIₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1.
I₀ = e − 1, I₁ = e − (e − 1) = 1 and I₂ = e − 2.

examples.title: Arc length of a catenary
examples.q: Find the length of the curve y = cosh x from x = 0 to x = ln 2.
steps: dy/dx = sinh x, so 1 + (dy/dx)² = 1 + sinh²x = cosh²x.
s = ∫ cosh x dx from 0 to ln 2 = sinh(ln 2).

examples.title: A surface of revolution
examples.q: The arc of y = x³ from x = 0 to x = 1 is rotated through 2π about the x-axis. Find the exact surface area.

fills.q: Iₙ = ∫ cosⁿx dx from 0 to π/2, with Iₙ = ((n − 1)/n)Iₙ₋₂ and I₀ = π/2.
Arc length of y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.
Arc length of y = cosh x from −ln 2 to ln 2.

exam.stem: Iₙ = ∫ xⁿ sin x dx from 0 to π/2, n ≥ 0.

parts.q: Show that Iₙ = n(π/2)ⁿ⁻¹ − n(n − 1)Iₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2.
ms: integrates by parts once: [−xⁿ cos x] + n∫ xⁿ⁻¹ cos x dx

parts.q: Find the exact value of I₄.
A curve has parametric equations x = t², y = ⅔t³, 0 ≤ t ≤ √3. Find the length of the curve.
The arc of y = √(4 − x²) between x = 0 and x = 1 is rotated through 2π about the x-axis. Find the exact area of the surface generated.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalisation
notes: An eigenvector v is non-zero and satisfies Av=λv. Eigenvalues solve det(A−λI)=0; then solve (A−λI)v=0 for each eigenspace. In 3×3 work, repeated eigenvalues do not automatically provide enough independent eigenvectors for diagonalisation.

Put independent eigenvectors into the columns of P in the same order as eigenvalues in D, so A=PDP⁻¹. Real symmetric matrices admit orthogonal diagonalisation with a suitable orthonormal eigenbasis. Normalisation changes an eigenvector’s length, not its direction or eigenvalue.

example.q: Diagonalise A=[[2,1],[1,2]].
steps: A=PDP⁻¹; normalised columns would give an orthogonal P.

practice.q: Find the eigenvalues and two independent eigenvectors of [[4,0],[0,−2]].
steps: The matrix is already diagonal in this basis.

check.q: What is the larger eigenvalue of [[2,1],[1,2]]?

deep.tip: Form det(A − λI) = 0, solve for the eigenvalues, then solve (A − λI)v = 0 separately for each one; any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is acceptable. Check with trace = sum of eigenvalues and determinant = product. For a symmetric matrix, normalise orthogonal eigenvectors so that P is orthogonal and PᵀAP = D.

examples.title: Diagonalising a 2 × 2 matrix
examples.q: Find P and D such that P⁻¹AP = D for A = [[3,1],[2,2]].

examples.title: Orthogonal diagonalisation
examples.q: A = [[2,0,0],[0,3,1],[0,1,3]]. Find an orthogonal matrix P and a diagonal matrix D with PᵀAP = D.
steps: det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)[(3 − λ)² − 1] = (2 − λ)²(4 − λ), so λ = 2 (twice) and 4.
λ = 2: y + z = 0 gives two orthogonal vectors (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, −1).

parts.q: Find the eigenvalues of A.
Find a corresponding eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
Write down matrices P and D such that P⁻¹AP = D.
ms: P = [[1,1],[1,−2]] with D = [[5,0],[0,2]] in the matching order

parts.q: Hence find A⁴.
Show that (1, 1, 0) is an eigenvector of C and state its eigenvalue.
Find the other eigenvalues of C.

ms: D = diag(3, −1, 3) in the matching order

parts.q: A 2 × 2 matrix A has eigenvalues 2 and −3 with corresponding eigenvectors (1, 0) and (1, 1). Find A.

lessons.title: Cayley–Hamilton and matrix powers
notes: Cayley–Hamilton states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. Replace the scalar variable by A and the constant term by a multiple of I. This gives recurrences for higher powers and can also express an inverse as a polynomial in A when the determinant is non-zero.

Check the sign convention used for the characteristic polynomial. Matrices generally do not commute, but powers of the same matrix do, so polynomial rearrangements in A are valid. Keep I in constant terms; subtracting a scalar from every entry is not matrix subtraction by a scalar multiple of I.

example.q: If A has characteristic polynomial λ²−5λ+6, express A³ in terms of A and I.

practice.q: For the same nonsingular A, express A⁻¹ in terms of A and I.
steps: The non-zero determinant 6 is consistent with invertibility.

check.q: If A²−5A+6I=0, find the coefficient of A in A³ expressed using only A and I.

deep.tip: Write the characteristic equation with λ replaced by A and the constant term multiplied by I. To reach a higher power, multiply through by A and substitute for A² repeatedly; to find an inverse, multiply through by A⁻¹, which is possible exactly when the constant term is non-zero.

examples.title: A square and an inverse
examples.q: A = [[2,1],[1,3]]. Use the Cayley–Hamilton theorem to express A² and A⁻¹ in terms of A and I.

examples.title: A 3 × 3 matrix
examples.q: A = [[1,1,0],[0,2,1],[0,0,3]]. Express A³ and A⁻¹ in terms of A², A and I.
steps: A is triangular, so its eigenvalues are 1, 2, 3 and the characteristic equation is (λ − 1)(λ − 2)(λ − 3) = 0.

parts.q: Find the characteristic equation of A.
Hence express A⁴ in the form pA + qI.
Express A⁻¹ in the form rA + sI.
Show that the characteristic equation of A is λ³ − 5λ² + 7λ − 3 = 0.
Hence find A⁻¹ in terms of A², A and I.

exam.stem: A 2 × 2 matrix A satisfies A² − 4A + 3I = 0.

parts.q: Find A⁴ in the form pA + qI.
Explain why A is non-singular and find A⁻¹ in terms of A and I.

lessons.title: Complex mappings and transformed regions
notes: A complex mapping w=f(z) transforms points and loci between two Argand planes. Write z=x+iy or invert the mapping in a useful form, substitute into the original locus and identify any excluded points. Fractional linear mappings can turn lines and circles into lines or circles.

The equation |z−a|=k|z−b| is an Apollonius locus, usually a circle when k≠1 and a perpendicular bisector when k=1. Argument inequalities select regions or angular sectors and require attention to branch boundaries and points where the relevant quotient is undefined.

example.q: Under w=1/z, find the image of the line Re(z)=1.
steps: The image is that circle excluding w=0, since 1/z cannot be zero for finite z.

practice.q: Under w=z², find the image of z=iy with y real.
steps: The image is the non-positive real axis, including zero.

check.q: Under w=z², what is Re(w) when z=2i?

deep.tip: Make z the subject (z in terms of w), substitute into the equation of the locus in the z-plane, and then put w = u + iv and simplify. Lines and circles map to lines and circles under w = 1/z and under fractional linear maps; check a couple of individual points to confirm the image and spot any excluded point.

examples.title: A circle through the origin under w = 1/z
examples.q: Find the image of the circle |z − 1| = 1 under w = 1/z.
steps: The points w are equidistant from 0 and 1.
The image is the line Re(w) = ½ (the point z = 0 has no image).

examples.title: An enlargement and translation
examples.q: Find the image of |z| = 1 under w = 2z + 1 − i.
steps: The image is the circle |w − (1 − i)| = 2: centre 1 − i, radius 2.

examples.title: A sector under w = z²
examples.q: Find the image of the region |z| ≤ 2, 0 ≤ arg z ≤ π/4 under w = z².
steps: In polar form, |w| = |z|² and arg w = 2 arg z.
The image is the quarter disc of radius 4 in the first quadrant.

fills.q: w = z² and arg z = π/6.

exam.stem: T maps z to w, where w = 1/z, z ≠ 0.

parts.q: Show that T maps the line Im(z) = 1 onto a circle, and find its centre and radius.
State the point on this circle that is not the image of any point on the line.
