parts.q: Show that T maps the imaginary axis onto the circle |w| = 1.

parts.q: Find the image of the region Re(z) > 0.
ms: these points are closer to 1 than to −1

lessons.title: Euclidean algorithm, Bézout and congruences
notes: The division algorithm reduces the greatest-common-divisor problem to smaller remainders. Back-substitution expresses the gcd as an integer combination of the original numbers: Bézout’s identity. A multiplicative inverse of a modulo n exists exactly when gcd(a,n)=1.

A congruence ax≡b modulo n is solvable precisely when gcd(a,n) divides b. Dividing a congruence by a common factor changes the modulus, so ordinary cancellation without checking conditions can lose solutions. Give all residue classes required by the question.

example.q: Find an inverse of 7 modulo 26.

practice.q: Solve 5x≡3 modulo 12.
steps: The inverse of 5 is 5 because 25≡1 modulo 12.

check.q: Find gcd(26,7).

deep.tip: Run Euclid’s algorithm as a column of equations, then reverse it one line at a time to write the gcd as a combination of the original numbers. A linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) has solutions only if gcd(a, n) divides b, and then it has exactly gcd(a, n) solutions modulo n.

examples.title: Euclid and Bézout
examples.q: Find gcd(252, 198) and integers a and b with 252a + 198b = gcd(252, 198).

examples.title: Solving a congruence with an inverse
examples.q: Solve 11x ≡ 4 (mod 17).

examples.title: A congruence with several solutions
examples.q: Solve 6x ≡ 9 (mod 15).
steps: gcd(6, 15) = 3 divides 9, so there are 3 solutions modulo 15.

parts.q: Use Euclid’s algorithm to find the highest common factor of 391 and 299.
Hence find integers a and b such that 391a + 299b = 23.
Solve the congruence 23x ≡ 5 (mod 40).
ms: finds the inverse of 23 modulo 40 by Euclid or trial

parts.q: Find all solutions of 8x ≡ 6 (mod 14), with 0 ≤ x < 14.
Explain why 8x ≡ 5 (mod 14) has no solutions.

lessons.title: Fermat, divisibility and combinatorial counting
notes: For prime p and a not divisible by p, Fermat’s little theorem gives a^(p−1)≡1 modulo p. Reduce the exponent only after checking that condition. Divisibility tests use place-value congruences; for 11, alternating digit sums arise from 10≡−1 modulo 11.

Use permutations when positions or order matter and combinations when only membership matters. Complement counting is often simpler than listing overlaps; inclusion–exclusion avoids double-counting. State whether repetitions and leading zeroes are allowed before forming a product.

example.q: Find the least non-negative residue of 3²⁰ modulo 7 and count 3-person teams from 8 people.
steps: For a team, order does not matter.

practice.q: How many length-3 digit strings contain at least one 7, if leading zeroes and repeats are allowed?
steps: This counts strings, not necessarily three-digit integers.

check.q: Find the least non-negative residue of 3²⁰ modulo 7.

deep.tip: For powers, reduce the exponent using Fermat’s little theorem (aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 mod p when p is prime and does not divide a) before calculating. For counting, decide whether order matters and whether items repeat; divide by the factorials of repeated letters, and handle restrictions by fixing the restricted positions first.

examples.title: Fermat’s little theorem
examples.q: Find the remainder when 5¹⁰⁰ is divided by 13.
steps: 13 is prime and does not divide 5, so 5¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13).

examples.title: A divisibility test
examples.q: Use the divisibility test for 11 to decide whether 7392 is divisible by 11.
steps: 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), so a number is congruent to the alternating sum of its digits.

examples.title: Arrangements with repeated letters
examples.q: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of BANANA?
steps: 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N repeated twice.

parts.q: Use Fermat’s little theorem to find the remainder when 3¹⁰² is divided by 11.
Prove that n⁵ − n is divisible by 5 for every integer n.
ms: if 5 ∤ n, Fermat gives n⁴ ≡ 1, so n⁵ ≡ n
if 5 | n, both terms are multiples of 5; so 5 | n⁵ − n for all n

exam.stem: The letters of the word STATISTICS are arranged in a line.

parts.q: Find the number of different arrangements.
Find the number of arrangements that begin and end with S.
How many four-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) have four different digits?
How many of these are divisible by 5?

lessons.title: First- and second-order recurrences and induction
notes: A linear recurrence combines a homogeneous solution with a particular solution. A constant equilibrium solves L=aL+b for uₙ₊₁=auₙ+b when a≠1. Subtracting that equilibrium reduces the recurrence to geometric form.

For a second-order recurrence, solve its characteristic equation and apply the two starting values. A repeated root needs a factor linear in n. Prove a proposed formula by checking the required initial cases and substituting it into the recurrence; a finite list of matching values is not a proof.

example.q: Solve uₙ₊₁=2uₙ+3 with u₀=1.
steps: An equilibrium satisfies L=2L+3, giving L=−3.

practice.q: Solve uₙ₊₂=3uₙ₊₁−2uₙ with u₀=0 and u₁=1.
steps: Characteristic roots satisfy r²−3r+2=0, so r=1,2.
A+B=0 and A+2B=1 give A=−1, B=1.
Check the initial values and substitution into the recurrence.

check.q: If uₙ=2ⁿ−1, find u₄.

deep.tip: For a homogeneous linear recurrence, solve the auxiliary equation and choose the form that matches its roots (distinct, repeated or complex). For a non-homogeneous one, add a particular solution shaped like the extra term, then use the initial terms on the complete general solution; check one term directly from the recurrence.

examples.title: A repeated auxiliary root
examples.q: Solve uₙ₊₂ = 4uₙ₊₁ − 4uₙ with u₀ = 1 and u₁ = 4.
steps: Auxiliary equation m² − 4m + 4 = 0 has the repeated root 2.
u₀ = 1 gives A = 1; u₁ = 2(1 + B) = 4 gives B = 1.

examples.title: A first-order recurrence with a linear term
examples.q: Solve uₙ₊₁ = 3uₙ + 2n with u₀ = 1.
steps: Try uₙ = an + b: a(n + 1) + b = 3an + 3b + 2n gives a = −1 and b = −½.
uₙ = C × 3ⁿ − n − ½, and u₀ = 1 gives C = 3/2.
uₙ = (3ⁿ⁺¹ − 2n − 1)/2; check u₁ = 3 from the recurrence.

exam.stem: uₙ₊₂ = uₙ₊₁ + 6uₙ, with u₀ = 2 and u₁ = 1.

parts.q: Find uₙ in terms of n.
Find u₅.

parts.q: Find Pₙ in terms of n.
Find the first year in which the population exceeds 6000.

exam.stem: uₙ₊₁ = 2uₙ + 3ⁿ, with u₀ = 0.

parts.q: Find uₙ in terms of n.
Prove your result by induction.

lessons.title: Discrete distributions, expectation and variance
notes: A discrete probability distribution assigns non-negative probabilities summing to one. Compute E(X)=Σxp(x) and Var(X)=E(X²)−E(X)²; square the outcomes in the first term, not the probabilities. A transformation changes both the possible values and their probabilities.

For Y=aX+b, the mean becomes aE(X)+b and the variance becomes a²Var(X). Adding a constant shifts every outcome without changing the spread. Independence is not needed for this single-variable transformation, but matters when combining different variables.

example.q: X takes 0,1,2 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Find its mean and variance.

practice.q: X takes 1,2,3 with probabilities 1/2,1/3,1/6. Find E(X) and Var(X).

check.q: A variable takes 0,1,2 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Find its mean.

deep.tip: Use ΣP(X = x) = 1 first to find any unknown probability. Work out E(X) and E(X²) in a table, then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². For a linear function, the constant shifts the mean only and the multiplier is squared in the variance.

examples.title: An unknown constant
examples.q: P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find k, E(X) and Var(X).

examples.title: Expectation of a function
examples.q: For the distribution in the previous example, find E(1/X) and Var(2X + 5).
steps: E(1/X) = 0.4; note that this is not 1/E(X).

exam.stem: X takes the values −1, 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.1, a, 0.3, b respectively, and E(X) = 0.8.

parts.q: Find the values of a and b.
Find Var(X).
Find Var(5 − 2X).

parts.q: Find the expected profit for one game.

parts.q: Find the variance of the profit.

parts.q: Find the values of a and b.

lessons.title: Poisson models and binomial approximation
notes: A Poisson model counts events in a specified interval with constant average rate and independent occurrences. Its mean and variance are both λ, and P(X=k)=e⁻λ λᵏ/k!. Scale λ when changing the interval before evaluating a probability.

A Poisson approximation to Bin(n,p) uses λ=np when n is large and p is small. Check the context and approximation quality rather than treating a rule of thumb as a theorem. Independent Poisson counts add their rates; a difference of counts is not generally Poisson.

example.q: Calls arrive at a mean rate of 2 per hour. Under a Poisson model, find P(no calls in 30 minutes).
steps: The model assumes the rate is stable and occurrences are independent.

practice.q: If X~Poisson(3), find P(X≤1).

check.q: A Poisson rate is 6 per hour. What is λ for 20 minutes?

deep.tip: Scale the mean to the interval in the question before calculating anything, and write the event as an inequality so the cumulative probability you need is clear. Poisson modelling needs events that occur singly, independently and at a constant average rate; the approximation to a binomial needs n large and p small.

examples.title: An upper tail
examples.q: X ~ Po(4.5). Find P(X ≥ 3).

examples.title: Adding independent Poisson variables
examples.q: Flaws of type A occur at a rate of 1.2 per metre and flaws of type B at 0.8 per metre, independently. Find the probability of exactly 2 flaws in a metre.
steps: The total number of flaws is Po(1.2 + 0.8) = Po(2).

examples.title: Approximating a binomial
examples.q: X ~ B(200, 0.015). Use a Poisson approximation to find P(X ≤ 2).
steps: n is large and p is small, so X ≈ Po(np) = Po(3).

exam.stem: Emails arrive at an average rate of 2.4 per 10 minutes and are modelled by a Poisson distribution.

parts.q: Find the probability of exactly 3 emails in a 10-minute period.
Find the probability of at least 2 emails in a 5-minute period.
State two assumptions needed for the Poisson model.
ms: emails arrive independently of one another
emails arrive singly and at a constant average rate

exam.stem: A machine makes components, each defective with probability 0.01 independently. X is the number of defective components in a batch of 400.

parts.q: Explain why a Poisson approximation is suitable.
ms: n = 400 is large and p = 0.01 is small

parts.q: Use the approximation to find P(X > 5).

exam.stem: X ~ Po(λ) and P(X = 2) = 3P(X = 0).

parts.q: Find the exact value of λ.
Find P(X = 1), to 4 decimal places.

lessons.title: Geometric and negative binomial waiting times
notes: With independent trials and success probability p, the geometric variable counting trials to the first success has support 1,2,… and P(X=k)=(1−p)^(k−1)p. Its mean is 1/p and variance (1−p)/p². State the counting convention before applying a formula.

For the trial number X of the rth success, P(X=k)=C(k−1,r−1)pʳ(1−p)^(k−r), k≥r. The final trial must be a success; the preceding k−1 trials contain r−1 successes. The mean and variance are r/p and r(1−p)/p².

example.q: Success probability is 1/4. Find the probability that the first success is on trial 3 and the mean waiting time.
steps: These counts include the successful trial.

practice.q: For independent fair trials with success probability 1/2, find the probability that the third success occurs on trial 5.
steps: Choose 2 successes among the first 4 trials: C(4,2)=6.

check.q: For a geometric waiting time counting the successful trial, p=0.2. Find E(X).

deep.tip: Decide what is being counted: the number of trials up to and including the first success is geometric, and up to and including the rth success is negative binomial. For the negative binomial the final trial must be a success, so the binomial coefficient counts arrangements of the earlier r − 1 successes only.

examples.title: Geometric probabilities
examples.q: X ~ Geo(0.2). Find P(X ≤ 4), P(X > 6) and Var(X).
steps: P(X > n) = (1 − p)ⁿ, since the first n trials all fail.

examples.title: A negative binomial probability
examples.q: Each trial succeeds with probability 0.3. Find the probability that the third success occurs on the eighth trial, and the mean and variance of the number of trials needed.
steps: Two successes in the first 7 trials, then a success on trial 8.

fills.q: Number of trials to the 4th success with p = 0.5.

parts.q: Find the probability that the first six occurs on the fourth throw.
Find the probability that more than five throws are needed.

parts.q: Find the probability that her second hit is on her fifth shot.

parts.q: Find the expected number of shots needed to obtain three hits.
Find the variance of the number of shots needed to obtain three hits.

parts.q: Find the value of p.
Find P(X ≥ 3).

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests for discrete distributions
notes: State a null model and an alternative before calculating a tail probability. A one-sided alternative chooses one tail; a two-sided alternative requires both directions to be handled using the specified testing convention. A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis, not the probability that the null is true.

A critical region contains outcomes causing rejection, and its actual probability under the null is the test’s size. A discrete model may not permit an exact nominal size. Report the decision in context and distinguish insufficient evidence from proof of the null.

example.q: Under H₀, X~Poisson(1). For H₁: λ>1, assess an observed count of 4 at the 5% level.
steps: It is below 0.05, so reject H₀.
There is evidence of an increased mean count under the model assumptions.

practice.q: Under H₀, X~Bin(4,1/2). For H₁:p>1/2, assess X=4 at the 5% level.
steps: The maximum observed count does not automatically imply a significant result.

check.q: Under Bin(4,1/2), find P(X=4).

deep.tip: State the hypotheses in terms of the parameter, and give the distribution of the test statistic under H₀ with the mean scaled to the period observed. Compare a tail probability (the observed value or more extreme) with the significance level, never a single-value probability, and word the conclusion in context without claiming proof.

examples.title: A one-tailed Poisson test
examples.q: Faults occur at a rate of 5 per week. After maintenance there is 1 fault in a week. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has decreased.
steps: H₀: λ = 5, H₁: λ < 5, with X ~ Po(5) under H₀.
There is evidence at the 5% level that the rate of faults has decreased.

examples.title: A two-tailed critical region
examples.q: X ~ Po(λ). Find the critical region for testing H₀: λ = 8 against H₁: λ ≠ 8 at the 5% level, with at most 2.5% in each tail, and state the actual significance level.
steps: Lower tail: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0138 and P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0424, so the region is X ≤ 2.
Upper tail: P(X ≥ 14) = 0.0342 and P(X ≥ 15) = 0.0173, so the region is X ≥ 15.

fills.q: A one-tailed test at the 5% level.
lines: reject H₀ when the tail probability is less than [[0.05]]

fills.q: A two-tailed test at the 10% level.

exam.stem: Accidents at a junction occurred at a mean rate of 3 per month. After new signs are installed there are 9 accidents in 6 months.

parts.q: Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether the mean rate of accidents has decreased. State your hypotheses clearly.
ms: under H₀ the 6-month count is Po(18)
0.0154 < 0.05: reject H₀; evidence that the rate has decreased

exam.stem: X is the number of attempts needed to obtain a first success, so X ~ Geo(p). A test of H₀: p = 0.2 against H₁: p < 0.2 is carried out at the 5% level.

parts.q: Find the critical region.
The first success occurs on the 12th attempt. State the conclusion of the test.
ms: 12 is not in the critical region: insufficient evidence that p is less than 0.2

exam.stem: X ~ Po(λ). A test of H₀: λ = 4 against H₁: λ > 4 is carried out at the 1% level.

parts.q: Find the critical region.
State the actual significance level of the test.

lessons.title: The central limit theorem and sample means
notes: For independent identically distributed observations with finite mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean has mean μ and variance σ²/n. The central limit theorem gives an approximate normal distribution for a sufficiently large sample, with the adequacy depending on the population’s shape.

The standard deviation of a sample mean is σ/√n, not σ/n. For a sum, multiply the mean by n and the variance by n. Check independence and whether a few extreme observations undermine a small-sample approximation. The theorem concerns the sampling distribution, not the shape of the original data.

example.q: A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. Approximate P(sample mean >54) for n=36 independent observations.
steps: The sample mean is approximately N(50,4).

practice.q: A population has variance 81. Find the standard deviation of the mean of 25 independent observations.
steps: The normal approximation, if used, needs an additional adequacy check.

check.q: If σ=12 and n=36, find the standard deviation of the sample mean.

deep.tip: Write down the mean and variance of the population first, then the distribution of the sample mean: mean μ and variance σ²/n. The central limit theorem is what allows a normal model when the population is not normal, and it needs a large sample; say so when you use it.

examples.title: Sample mean of Poisson data
examples.q: X ~ Po(2.5). A random sample of 40 observations is taken. Estimate the probability that the sample mean exceeds 2.9.
steps: The population has mean 2.5 and variance 2.5.
By the central limit theorem the sample mean is approximately N(2.5, 2.5/40) = N(2.5, 0.0625).

examples.title: Scores on a die
examples.q: A fair die is rolled 50 times. Estimate the probability that the mean score is at least 3.8.
steps: One roll has mean 3.5 and variance 35/12.
The sample mean is approximately N(3.5, 35/600), with standard error 0.2415.

exam.stem: X ~ Geo(0.25), so that E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 12. A random sample of 48 observations of X is taken.

parts.q: State the approximate distribution of the sample mean.
Estimate the probability that the sample mean is less than 3.5.
Explain why the normal approximation is appropriate.
ms: the sample is large, so the central limit theorem applies

parts.q: The masses of loaves have mean 250 g and standard deviation 8 g. Estimate the probability that the mean mass of a random sample of 64 loaves lies between 248 g and 251 g.
ms: standardises both values: z = −2 and z = 1

parts.q: A population has standard deviation 6. Find the smallest sample size for which the probability that the sample mean lies within 1 of the population mean is at least 0.95.

lessons.title: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit and independence
notes: The chi-squared statistic is Σ(O−E)²/E. Expected counts come from the null model, not from rounding observed proportions to convenient values. For independence in a contingency table, E=(row total×column total)/grand total.

Use suitable expected frequencies, combining categories where justified before testing. Degrees of freedom for a goodness-of-fit test are categories−1−parameters estimated from the data; for an r×c independence table they are (r−1)(c−1). Reject for sufficiently large values of the statistic and state the evidence in context.

example.q: Four equally likely categories have observed counts 18,22,16,24. Calculate the chi-squared statistic.
steps: Total=80, so every expected count is 20.
There are 4−1=3 degrees of freedom if no parameters were estimated.
A test decision requires the chosen significance level and its critical value.

practice.q: A 2×3 contingency table has suitable expected counts. State its degrees of freedom and explain how each expected count is found.
steps: Each expected count is row total times column total divided by grand total.
Use observed counts only in the numerator of each (O−E)²/E contribution.
The null hypothesis is independence of the two categorical variables.

check.q: A goodness-of-fit test has 5 categories and estimates no parameters. Find its degrees of freedom.

deep.tip: Expected frequencies come from the null hypothesis and must add up to the observed total; combine classes until each expected frequency is at least 5. Degrees of freedom are the number of classes after combining, minus 1, minus one more for each parameter estimated from the data; for a contingency table use (rows − 1)(columns − 1).

examples.title: Goodness of fit for a die
examples.q: A die is rolled 60 times, giving frequencies 8, 12, 9, 11, 6, 14 for the scores 1 to 6. Test at the 5% level whether the die is fair.
steps: H₀: each score has probability ⅙. Each expected frequency is 10.
Degrees of freedom = 6 − 1 = 5; the 5% critical value is 11.070.
4.2 < 11.070: do not reject H₀; the data are consistent with a fair die.

examples.title: A 2 × 2 contingency table
examples.q: Of 50 people given treatment A, 30 improved; of 50 given treatment B, 10 improved. Test at the 5% level whether improvement is independent of treatment.
steps: H₀: improvement is independent of treatment. Column totals are 40 improved and 60 not.
Expected: 50 × 40/100 = 20 improved and 30 not improved in each row.
16.67 > 3.841: reject H₀; improvement is associated with treatment.

fills.q: Row total 40, column total 30, grand total 120.
Five classes with one parameter estimated from the data.

exam.stem: The number of goals scored in each of 100 matches was recorded: 0 goals in 22 matches, 1 in 34, 2 in 26, 3 in 12, and 4 or more in 6. The mean of the data is 1.5. A Poisson model is to be tested.

parts.q: Show that the expected frequency for 2 goals is 25.10.
Explain why there are 3 degrees of freedom.
ms: 5 classes, each with expected frequency at least 5
5 − 1 − 1, because the totals agree and the mean was estimated

parts.q: The other expected frequencies are 22.31, 33.47, 12.55 and 6.56. Calculate the test statistic.
Complete the test at the 5% level.
ms: 0.118 < 7.815: do not reject H₀; a Poisson model is consistent with the data

exam.stem: 120 students were classified by year group and by the lunch option they chose. Year 12: 20 hot, 30 cold, 10 none. Year 13: 10 hot, 20 cold, 30 none.

lessons.title: Probability generating functions and sums
notes: For a non-negative integer-valued variable, G(t)=E(tˣ)=Σpₖtᵏ. The coefficient of tᵏ is P(X=k), so the powers encode outcomes and the coefficients encode their probabilities. G(1)=1, G′(1)=E(X), and G″(1)=E[X(X−1)]. Therefore Var(X)=G″(1)+G′(1)−[G′(1)]².

Independent sums have a generating function equal to the product of the individual generating functions. This product rule depends on independence. Obtain probabilities from coefficients or derivatives at zero, not from substituting the outcome into G.

example.q: For G(t)=(1+2t+t²)/4, find the mean and variance.
steps: The coefficients are valid probabilities and G(1)=1.

practice.q: Independent X and Y have PGFs (1+t)/2 and (1+t²)/2. Find the distribution of X+Y.
steps: Check that the probabilities sum to one.

check.q: What must a valid probability generating function equal at t=1?

deep.tip: The coefficient of tˣ in G(t) is P(X = x), so G(1) = 1 always. Use E(X) = G′(1) and Var(X) = G″(1) + G′(1) − [G′(1)]². For a sum of independent variables multiply the generating functions; multiplying is only valid when the variables are independent.

examples.title: Mean and variance from a PGF
examples.q: X has probability generating function G(t) = (0.4 + 0.6t)³. Find P(X = 2), E(X) and Var(X).
steps: The t² coefficient is 3 × 0.4 × 0.6² = 0.432, so P(X = 2) = 0.432.

examples.title: Sum of independent Poisson variables
examples.q: X ~ Po(2) and Y ~ Po(3) are independent. Use generating functions to find the distribution of X + Y.
steps: For independent variables, G_(X+Y)(t) = G_X(t) G_Y(t).
This is the generating function of Po(5), so X + Y ~ Po(5).

lessons.title: Size, Type I and Type II errors, and power
notes: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis; its probability is the size of the test. A Type II error fails to reject a false null, and its probability depends on a specified alternative parameter value. Power at that alternative is one minus the Type II error probability.

Use the same fixed critical region when calculating size and power, but change the probability model to the null or specified alternative as appropriate. Increasing the sample size can improve power without increasing the nominal size. A high p-value is not evidence that the Type II error probability is small.

example.q: A test observes X~Bin(4,p) and rejects H₀:p=1/2 only if X=4. Find its size and power at p=0.8.
steps: The Type II error probability there is 1−0.4096=0.5904.
This is a 6.25% size test, not a 5% test.

practice.q: For the same rejection rule, find the power at p=0.9.

check.q: If a test has Type II error probability 0.3 at an alternative, what is its power there?

deep.tip: Fix the critical region first: size and power are both probabilities of landing in that region, calculated under different parameter values. Size uses the value in H₀; power uses a particular value from H₁; and P(Type II error) = 1 − power. A power function is the same calculation left in terms of the parameter.

examples.title: Size and power of a Poisson test
examples.q: X ~ Po(λ). H₀: λ = 3 is tested against H₁: λ > 3 and H₀ is rejected when X ≥ 7. Find the size of the test and its power when λ = 6.

examples.title: A power function
examples.q: X ~ B(10, p). H₀: p = 0.5 is tested against H₁: p < 0.5 and H₀ is rejected when X ≤ 1. Find the size, the power function, and the power when p = 0.2.
steps: Power function = P(X ≤ 1 | p) = (1 − p)¹⁰ + 10p(1 − p)⁹.

X ~ Po(3) and H₀ is rejected only when X = 0.

Find the power of the test when p = 0.7.

lessons.title: Least squares, residuals and regression inference
notes: A least-squares line of y on x minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals. Its slope is Sxy/Sxx and it passes through (x̄,ȳ). The regression of x on y minimises different residuals and is not generally obtained by rearranging the first line.

Residual plots can reveal curvature or changing variability. Inference for a slope requires a suitable linear-error model, normally with independent errors of constant variance and normality for small-sample t procedures. Distinguish prediction within the observed range from unsupported extrapolation.

example.q: Given x̄=4, ȳ=9, Sxx=10 and Sxy=25, find the regression line and the residual at (5,13).
steps: At x=5 the fitted value is 11.5.

practice.q: Given x̄=2, ȳ=7, Sxx=8 and Sxy=12, find the regression of y on x.

check.q: Given Sxy=25 and Sxx=10, find the slope of the least-squares line of y on x.

deep.tip: Compute Sxx and Sxy from the summary statistics first; then b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − bx̄, because the regression line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). A residual is observed minus predicted; the residual sum of squares is Syy − Sxy²/Sxx, and a pattern in the residuals suggests that a linear model is unsuitable.

steps: The line explains 40 of the 50 units of variation in y.

lessons.title: Densities, distribution functions and continuous models
notes: A density is non-negative and has total integral one. Probabilities are areas, so P(X=x)=0 for an individual value in a continuous model. A distribution function F(x)=P(X≤x) is non-decreasing and includes the appropriate constant pieces outside the support.

Moments are obtained by integrating x f(x) and x² f(x), and Var(X)=E(X²)−E(X)². Uniform and exponential models have specific support and assumptions. For Y=g(X), transform probability events or the CDF carefully; a non-monotonic mapping can have more than one inverse branch.

example.q: For f(x)=2x on 0≤x≤1 and zero elsewhere, find F(x) on the support and E(X).

practice.q: For the same density, find Var(X) and P(X>1/2).
steps: A point endpoint has zero probability.

check.q: For f(x)=2x on [0,1], find F(1/2).

deep.tip: Use ∫f(x) dx = 1 over the support to find any constant, and remember that probabilities are areas, so P(X = a) = 0. Move between f and F by integrating and differentiating; the median m satisfies F(m) = ½, the mode is where f is greatest, and Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

examples.q: X has density f(x) = kx(2 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find k, E(X) and Var(X).
steps: k∫ (2x − x²) dx from 0 to 2 = k(4 − 8/3) = 4k/3 = 1, so k = ¾.
The density is symmetric about x = 1, so E(X) = 1.

examples.q: X ~ U[2, 8]. Find E(X), Var(X) and P(X > 6.5).

lessons.title: Product moment, rank correlation and tests
notes: The product moment correlation coefficient measures linear association using centred products; Spearman’s coefficient measures monotonic association through ranks. With no ties, Spearman’s formula is 1−6Σd²/[n(n²−1)]. With tied observations use appropriate average ranks and the required method.

A significance test needs the correct null model, alternative, sample size and critical value or p-value. Statistical association does not establish causation. Population bivariate normal assumptions matter for standard small-sample inference about Pearson correlation, and a scatter plot can reveal a misleading outlier.

example.q: For four untied paired ranks, Σd²=2. Find Spearman’s coefficient.
steps: This indicates positive rank association, not proof of a causal relationship.

practice.q: For five untied paired ranks, Σd²=4. Calculate Spearman’s coefficient.
steps: A significance conclusion needs a specified test and critical value.

check.q: For n=4 untied ranks with Σd²=2, find Spearman correlation.

deep.tip: Use the product moment coefficient r = Sxy/√(SxxSyy) for a linear relationship between bivariate normal data, and Spearman’s rank coefficient when the data are ranks or the relationship is monotonic but not linear. In a test, compare the coefficient with the critical value for the sample size, tail and significance level, and state the conclusion in context.

There is evidence of positive correlation.

lessons.title: Linear combinations of random variables
notes: Expectation is linear whether or not variables are independent. Variance includes covariance: Var(aX+bY)=a²Var(X)+b²Var(Y)+2abCov(X,Y). For independent variables the covariance term is zero; subtracting variables still adds their variances in that case.

Independent normal variables have normal linear combinations. For other populations, an exact normal conclusion needs justification or an adequate approximation. State independence explicitly when using a sum of variances, and use standard deviations only after calculating the variance.

example.q: Independent X~N(10,4) and Y~N(3,1). Find the distribution of 2X−Y.
steps: Therefore 2X−Y~N(17,17), where the second parameter is variance.

practice.q: X and Y have variances 9 and 4 and covariance 2. Find Var(X−2Y).
steps: Ignoring covariance would give the incorrect value 25.

check.q: Independent X and Y have variances 4 and 1. Find Var(2X−Y).

deep.tip: Write the mean and the variance of the combination separately: E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y), and for independent variables Var(aX + bY) = a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y), so the variances add even when the variables are subtracted. Distinguish 3X (one value tripled, variance 9σ²) from X₁ + X₂ + X₃ (three independent values, variance 3σ²).

steps: Var(X₁ + X₂ + X₃) = σ² + σ² + σ² = 3σ².
Tripling one value is more variable than adding three independent values.

lessons.title: Normal means, confidence intervals and two-sample tests
notes: For independent observations from a normal population with known variance, standardise a sample mean using σ/√n. A two-sided 95% confidence interval is x̄±1.96σ/√n. Confidence describes the long-run coverage of the procedure, not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed population mean.

For two independent means, the variance of their difference is σ₁²/n₁+σ₂²/n₂. Large-sample approximations may replace unknown variances by sample estimates when justified. Do not use an independent-samples formula for paired observations from the same individuals.

example.q: A normal population has known σ=6. A sample of 36 has mean 20. Find a 95% interval for μ.
steps: This procedure has 95% coverage under the stated model.

practice.q: Independent means have sample sizes 25 and 16, with known population variances 9 and 4. Find the standard error of their difference.
steps: Both samples must be independent for this calculation.
Use this standard error with the appropriate normal critical value.

check.q: If known σ=6 and n=36, find the normal-theory standard error.

deep.tip: Find the standard error before anything else: σ/√n for one mean, √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂) for a difference of independent means. A confidence interval is estimate ± z × standard error; a test compares (estimate − hypothesised value)/standard error with a critical value. If the population is not normal, a large sample lets you use the central limit theorem.

examples.q: A normal population has σ = 4. A sample of 25 has mean 52.3. Find a 99% confidence interval for μ.

examples.q: Sample A: n = 40, mean 31.2, σ² = 16. Sample B: n = 50, mean 29.5, σ² = 25. Test at the 5% level whether μ_A > μ_B.
steps: H₀: μ_A = μ_B, H₁: μ_A > μ_B.
1.792 > 1.6449: reject H₀; evidence that the mean of A is greater.

The manufacturer claims the mean mass is 100 g. Comment on this claim.

ms: H₀: μ_A = μ_B, H₁: μ_A ≠ μ_B

ms: for a large sample the sample mean is approximately normally distributed, whatever the population distribution

lessons.title: Inference for variances and variance ratios
notes: For a random sample of size n from a normal population, (n−1)S²/σ² has a chi-squared distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom when S² uses denominator n−1. Rearrange the pivot carefully to form variance confidence limits; reciprocals reverse the critical-value order.

The ratio of two independent sample variances from normal populations can be tested with an F distribution. Preserve the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom associated with the chosen ratio. These exact procedures depend strongly on normality and independence.

example.q: For n=10 and S²=10, test H₀:σ²=4 against σ²>4 at 5%, using the supplied critical value 16.919.
steps: Under H₀ it is χ² with 9 degrees of freedom.
There is evidence of a larger variance under the normal model.

practice.q: Independent normal samples of sizes 8 and 11 have sample variances 12 and 4. Give the F statistic and its degrees of freedom for their ratio.
steps: Under equal population variances, the statistic has F(7,10).

check.q: For a normal sample of n=10, what are the degrees of freedom of the variance chi-squared pivot?

deep.tip: For one variance, (n − 1)S²/σ² has a χ² distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, so tests and confidence intervals both come from χ² tables; note that the interval is not symmetric. To compare two variances, put the larger sample variance on top of the F ratio and use degrees of freedom (numerator n − 1, denominator n − 1) in that order.

examples.q: A sample of 12 from a normal population has s² = 2.9. Test at the 5% level whether σ² > 1.5.
steps: 21.27 > 19.675: reject H₀; evidence that the variance exceeds 1.5.

examples.q: A sample of 10 from a normal population has s² = 4.2. Find a 95% confidence interval for σ².

steps: H₀: σ₁² = σ₂², H₁: σ₁² > σ₂².

An F-test with sample sizes 7 (numerator) and 10.

lessons.title: Student t, paired tests and pooled variances
notes: When a normal population variance is unknown, a one-sample mean statistic uses t=(x̄−μ₀)/(S/√n) with n−1 degrees of freedom. A paired test applies this procedure to the within-pair differences; the pairs, rather than all individual observations, form the independent sample.

A pooled two-sample t procedure assumes independent normal populations with equal variances. Pool using degrees-of-freedom weights, not a simple average unless sample sizes agree. Match the tail of the critical value to the alternative and keep a non-rejection conclusion appropriately cautious.

example.q: A normal sample of n=9 has mean 12 and S=3. Test μ=10 against μ≠10 at 5%, using critical value 2.306.
steps: There is insufficient evidence of a difference at 5%; this does not prove μ=10.

practice.q: Ten paired differences have mean 2 and standard deviation 3. Calculate the test statistic for a zero population mean difference.
steps: The analysis is on paired differences, not 20 independent measurements.

check.q: A one-sample t test uses 9 independent observations. Find its degrees of freedom.

deep.tip: Use the t-distribution when the population is normal but its variance is estimated from the sample. A one-sample or paired test has n − 1 degrees of freedom; a two-sample test with a pooled variance has n₁ + n₂ − 2. For paired data, work with the differences as a single sample.

lessons.title: Momentum, impulse and vector change
notes: Momentum is the vector mv, and impulse equals the change in momentum. Draw or state the positive direction before subtracting velocities. A force–time graph gives impulse as signed area; for a variable force use its time integral.

In an isolated collision, internal impulses cancel and total momentum is conserved over the short impact. Kinetic energy need not be conserved. In vector problems, apply the impulse–momentum relation component by component and report the impulse direction, not only its magnitude.

example.q: A 0.5 kg particle changes velocity from (4,−2) to (−2,6) m/s. Find the impulse.
steps: The vector specifies the impulse direction.

practice.q: A 2 kg particle moving at +3 m/s rebounds at −1 m/s. Find its impulse.
steps: The impulse acts opposite to the original positive direction.

check.q: A 0.5 kg particle has velocity change (−6,8) m/s. Find impulse magnitude in N s.

deep.tip: Choose a positive direction (or use vectors) and keep the signs of every velocity; impulse equals the change in momentum, m(v − u). In a collision or explosion, total momentum is conserved but kinetic energy usually is not, so find the velocities with momentum before you discuss energy.

examples.title: A rebounding ball
examples.q: A ball of mass 0.2 kg hits the ground at 8 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 5 m s⁻¹. Find the impulse exerted by the ground.
steps: Take upwards as positive: u = −8 and v = 5.

examples.q: A particle of mass 0.4 kg moving with velocity (5i + 2j) m s⁻¹ receives an impulse of (−3i + 4j) N s. Find its new velocity and speed.
steps: I = m(v − u), so v = u + I/m.

examples.title: Coalescing particles
examples.q: A particle of mass 3 kg moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with a particle of mass 2 kg moving at 1 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction, and they coalesce. Find their common velocity and the loss of kinetic energy.
steps: v = 2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 3 kg particle.
Kinetic energy before = 24 + 1 = 25 J; after = ½ × 5 × 2² = 10 J.

A 2 kg particle speeds up from 3 to 7 m s⁻¹ in a straight line.
A 4 kg particle moving at 2.5 m s⁻¹.

lessons.title: Work, energy and power
notes: Work by a constant force is the scalar product of force and displacement. For a variable force along a line, work is ∫F dx. The work–energy relation accounts for all relevant forces: a gain in kinetic energy is not necessarily equal to the work by the driving force alone.

Instantaneous power is F·v. A constant-power model therefore gives driving force P/v away from zero speed and may be unrealistic at rest. Include changes in gravitational potential energy and work against resistance with consistent signs.

example.q: A 2 kg particle speeds from 3 to 5 m/s while a resistance does 8 J of negative work. Find the work by the driving force.

practice.q: A force F(x)=3x² N acts along a displacement from x=0 to x=2 m. Find its work.

check.q: Find the kinetic energy increase for 2 kg changing speed from 3 to 5 m/s, in joules.

deep.tip: Write the work–energy principle as one equation: initial energy + work by driving forces = final energy + work against resistances, with each term in joules. For power, use P = Fv with the driving force F, then Newton’s second law for acceleration; maximum speed occurs when the driving force equals the total resistance.

examples.title: Power and acceleration
examples.q: A car of mass 900 kg moves on a level road against a resistance of 600 N. Its engine works at 18 kW. Find its acceleration when its speed is 15 m s⁻¹, and its maximum speed.
steps: At maximum speed F = 600, so v = 18 000/600 = 30 m s⁻¹.

examples.title: Work–energy on a rough slope
examples.q: A particle of mass 5 kg is released from rest and slides 4 m down a rough plane inclined at 30°. The coefficient of friction is 0.2. Find its speed.
steps: Loss of potential energy = 5g × 4 sin 30° = 98 J.
R = 5g cos 30° = 42.4 N, so friction = 0.2R = 8.49 N, doing 33.9 J of work.

fills.q: A driving force of 400 N at 25 m s⁻¹.
A 3 kg particle moving at 4 m s⁻¹.

exam.stem: A lorry of mass 4000 kg moves up a straight road inclined at α to the horizontal, where sin α = 1/20. The resistance to motion is 1500 N. The lorry moves at a constant speed of 12 m s⁻¹.

parts.q: Find the power of the engine.
The lorry reaches a level road. The power and the resistance are unchanged. Find the acceleration of the lorry at the instant its speed is 12 m s⁻¹.

A particle of mass 2 kg is projected up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 30° with speed 6 m s⁻¹. The coefficient of friction is 0.25. Use the work–energy principle to find how far up the plane the particle moves before coming to rest.
A pump raises 50 kg of water per second through a height of 12 m and ejects it at 8 m s⁻¹. Find the power of the pump.
ms: kinetic energy per second ½ × 50 × 8² = 1600 J

lessons.title: Elastic strings, springs and energy
notes: For a light elastic string of natural length l and modulus λ, tension is λx/l when extension x>0. A string is slack when compressed, whereas an ideal spring can push as well as pull. Elastic energy stored at extension x is λx²/(2l).

Choose the energy reference for gravitational potential and account for any slack stage before the string becomes taut. At a turning point the instantaneous speed is zero, but acceleration need not be zero. Check whether the calculated extension lies in the physical regime assumed.

example.q: A string has natural length 2 m and modulus 40 N. Find tension and elastic energy at extension 0.3 m.
steps: The total length is 2.3 m; extension is not the total length.

practice.q: An elastic spring has natural length 0.5 m and modulus 30 N. Find the energy stored when stretched to length 0.7 m.

check.q: For natural length 2 m, modulus 40 N and extension 0.3 m, find string tension in newtons.

deep.tip: Use Hooke’s law T = λx/l for forces and E = λx²/2l for energy, where x is the extension, not the stretched length. In energy problems list every form at the start and at the end: kinetic, gravitational and elastic. Remember that a string is slack (no tension) once it is shorter than its natural length.

examples.title: Equilibrium on an elastic string
examples.q: A particle of mass 2 kg hangs in equilibrium on an elastic string of natural length 1.5 m and modulus 49 N. Find the extension.

examples.title: Released from a spring
examples.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg on a smooth horizontal table is attached to a spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus 20 N. It is pulled out to an extension of 0.2 m and released. Find its speed as it passes through the natural length.
steps: At the natural length all of this is kinetic energy.

examples.title: Falling on an elastic string
examples.q: A particle of mass 1 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus 4g N, whose other end is fixed at O. The particle is dropped from O. Find its greatest extension.
steps: At the lowest point the particle is at rest, having fallen 1 + x metres.
Loss of potential energy = elastic energy: g(1 + x) = 4gx²/2.

fills.q: λ = 20 N, l = 1.5 m, extension 0.3 m.
λ = 30 N, l = 0.5 m, extension 0.2 m.
A 3 kg mass hangs on a string with λ = 147 N, l = 2 m (g = 9.8).

exam.stem: A particle of mass 0.4 kg hangs on a light elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus 9.8 N, attached to a fixed point.

parts.q: Find the extension of the string in equilibrium.
The particle is pulled down a further 0.1 m and released from rest. Find its speed as it passes through the equilibrium position.
ms: elastic energy at extensions 0.42 m and 0.32 m
includes the gain in potential energy 0.4g × 0.1

parts.q: A particle of mass 1.5 kg on a smooth horizontal surface is held against a spring of natural length 0.5 m and modulus 60 N, compressing it by 0.15 m. It is released. Find the speed with which it leaves the spring.

exam.stem: A bungee jumper of mass 70 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 20 m. The other end is fixed to a bridge. She falls from rest at the bridge and first comes to instantaneous rest 45 m below it.

parts.q: Find the modulus of elasticity of the rope.
ms: energy equation: loss of potential energy = elastic energy

parts.q: State one modelling assumption you have made.
ms: the jumper is a particle, or air resistance is negligible, or the rope is light

lessons.title: Direct collisions and Newton’s law of restitution
notes: For a direct collision use momentum conservation together with speed of separation=e×speed of approach. Write a signed velocity equation consistent with the ordering of the particles; using unsigned speeds too early can conceal a rebound.

The restitution coefficient satisfies 0≤e≤1 for the usual model. For successive collisions, finish the first event, update positions and velocities and check whether the next proposed collision can actually occur. Kinetic energy loss is non-negative in the ordinary two-particle model.

example.q: A 2 kg particle at 3 m/s strikes a stationary 1 kg particle. The coefficient of restitution is 1/2. Find velocities after impact.

practice.q: Two equal masses collide directly. Initial velocities are 4 and 0 m/s and e=1/2. Find the final velocities.
steps: Solve to get v₁=1 and v₂=3 m/s.
Check momentum and speed of separation.

check.q: Equal masses collide with u₁=4, u₂=0 and e=1/2. Find the speed of separation.

deep.tip: Draw before-and-after diagrams with every velocity arrow in the same positive direction, so an answer that comes out negative tells you the particle moves the other way. Use two equations: conservation of momentum and Newton’s law of restitution, written as separation speed = e × approach speed.

examples.title: A head-on collision
examples.q: A particle of mass 3 kg moving at 5 m s⁻¹ collides directly with a particle of mass 2 kg moving at 2 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The coefficient of restitution is 0.4. Find their velocities after the collision and the kinetic energy lost.
steps: Solving: v₁ = 1.08 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = 3.88 m s⁻¹, both in the original direction of the 3 kg particle.
Kinetic energy before = 41.5 J and after = 16.80 J, so 24.7 J is lost.

examples.title: Rebounding from a wall
examples.q: A sphere hits a smooth wall at right angles with speed 6 m s⁻¹ and e = ⅔. Find its speed after the impact and after a second impact with a parallel wall.
steps: After the first impact: ⅔ × 6 = 4 m s⁻¹.
Its speed is unchanged until it reaches the second wall.
After the second impact: ⅔ × 4 = 8/3 m s⁻¹.

fills.q: Equal masses, e = 1: A at 5 m s⁻¹ hits B at rest.
A ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ with e = 0.6.

exam.stem: Particles P and Q, of masses 2 kg and 4 kg, move in the same direction along a straight line with speeds 6 m s⁻¹ and 1 m s⁻¹. P collides with Q. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5.

parts.q: Find the speeds of P and Q after the collision.
Find the kinetic energy lost in the collision.
Q then hits a fixed wall at right angles, with coefficient of restitution 0.4. Show that P and Q collide again.
ms: P moves towards the wall and Q towards P, so they approach each other

exam.stem: A particle A of mass m moving with speed u collides directly with a particle B of mass 2m at rest. The coefficient of restitution is e.

parts.q: Show that the speed of B after the collision is u(1 + e)/3.
ms: eliminates v_A to obtain the given result

parts.q: Find the velocity of A after the collision, and the range of values of e for which A reverses its direction.

exam.stem: A ball of mass 0.3 kg moving horizontally at 8 m s⁻¹ hits a fixed vertical wall at right angles and rebounds at 5 m s⁻¹.

parts.q: Find the coefficient of restitution between the ball and the wall.
Find the magnitude of the impulse exerted by the wall.
Find the kinetic energy lost in the impact.

lessons.title: Oblique impacts and successive rebounds
notes: For impact with a smooth fixed plane, resolve velocity normal and parallel to the plane. The parallel component is unchanged; the normal component reverses and is multiplied by e. Recombine the components to obtain speed and angle after impact.

An impulsive force from a smooth surface acts normally. The energy loss arises from the normal component, not the whole incident speed. For successive impacts, use the new direction and check the geometry before applying the next normal–tangential decomposition.

example.q: A particle has velocity (3,−4) m/s and strikes the horizontal smooth line y=0. Let e=1/2. Find the rebound velocity.

practice.q: A particle with velocity (−6,8) strikes the vertical smooth line x=0 with e=1/3. Find the rebound velocity and speed.
steps: The normal x-component reverses and scales: −(1/3)(−6)=2.

check.q: A normal velocity component −4 rebounds from a smooth fixed wall with e=1/2. Find the outgoing normal component.

deep.tip: Resolve every velocity parallel and perpendicular to the surface, or along and perpendicular to the line of centres. Smooth contact means the parallel components are unchanged; restitution and (for two spheres) momentum act only along the normal or line of centres. Recombine at the end for speed and direction.

examples.title: Oblique impact with a wall
examples.q: A smooth sphere hits a smooth wall with speed 10 m s⁻¹ at 60° to the wall. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find its speed and direction after the impact.
steps: Perpendicular component 10 sin 60° = 8.66, reversed and multiplied by 0.5: 4.33.

examples.title: Using vectors
examples.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg moving with velocity (4i − 6j) m s⁻¹ hits a smooth fixed surface whose normal is parallel to j. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find its velocity after impact, the impulse and the loss of kinetic energy.
steps: The i-component is unchanged; the j-component becomes +0.5 × 6 = 3.

examples.title: Two spheres
examples.q: Smooth spheres A and B have equal mass. A moves with velocity (3i + 4j) m s⁻¹ and hits B, which is at rest. At impact the line of centres is parallel to i and e = ½. Find their velocities after the collision.
steps: Perpendicular to the line of centres, A keeps 4j and B has 0j.
Along i: momentum 3 = a + b; restitution b − a = ½ × 3.

fills.q: A smooth surface: parallel component 8 m s⁻¹.

exam.stem: A ball strikes a smooth horizontal floor with speed 12 m s⁻¹ at an angle of 30° to the floor. The coefficient of restitution is 0.6.

parts.q: Find the speed of the ball immediately after the impact.
Find the angle between the ball’s path and the floor after the impact.
Find the fraction of the ball’s kinetic energy lost.

exam.stem: Smooth spheres A (mass 2 kg) and B (mass 1 kg) have velocities (5i + 2j) m s⁻¹ and (−i + 3j) m s⁻¹. When they collide the line of centres is parallel to i, and e = ½.

parts.q: Find the velocities of A and B immediately after the collision.
Find the impulse on B.

exam.stem: A particle of mass 0.2 kg moving with velocity (8i + 6j) m s⁻¹ hits a smooth fixed wall whose normal is parallel to i. Its speed after the impact is 6.5 m s⁻¹.

parts.q: Find the coefficient of restitution.
Find the magnitude of the impulse on the particle.

lessons.title: Uniform and vertical circular motion
notes: Angular speed ω and tangential speed satisfy v=rω. The radial acceleration is v²/r towards the centre, so resolve forces in that inward direction rather than introducing a separate physical “centripetal force”. Gravity’s radial component changes around a vertical circle.

Combine energy conservation with the radial equation when speed varies with height. A string requires non-negative tension and a surface contact requires a non-negative normal reaction. The limiting loss-of-contact condition is found by setting that force to zero, then checking where it occurs.

example.q: A 0.5 kg particle moves on a horizontal smooth table in a circle of radius 2 m at speed 4 m/s, held by a string. Find tension.
steps: The string supplies the horizontal radial force.

practice.q: A particle on a light string completes a vertical circle of radius r. State the least speed at the top for a taut-string model.
steps: At the top, inward forces give T+mg=mv²/r.
The limiting taut condition is T=0.
Other positions must also satisfy the physical constraints.

check.q: Find radial acceleration for speed 4 m/s and radius 2 m, in m/s².

deep.tip: Mark the centre of the circle and resolve towards it: the resultant inward force equals mv²/r = mrω². In a vertical circle, energy links the speeds at different heights; a string stays taut while the tension is positive, whereas a particle on a rigid rod or inside a tube only needs speed at the top.

examples.title: A conical pendulum
examples.q: A particle of mass 0.2 kg on a string of length 0.5 m moves in a horizontal circle with the string at 30° to the vertical. Find the tension and the angular speed.
steps: Vertically: T cos 30° = 0.2g, so T = 2.263 N.

examples.title: A vertical circle
examples.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg on a string of length 0.8 m is moving in a vertical circle. Its speed at the lowest point is 7 m s⁻¹. Find its speed and the tension at the highest point.
steps: T = 6.125 N; positive, so the string is taut.

examples.title: A banked track
examples.q: A car travels round a smooth track banked at 20° in a horizontal circle of radius 50 m. Find the speed at which there is no tendency to slip.

fills.q: ω = 3 rad s⁻¹ and r = 2 m.
v = 4 m s⁻¹ and r = 2 m.
lines: acceleration towards the centre = [[8]] m s⁻²

parts.q: A car moves on a horizontal circular track of radius 60 m. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the track is 0.5. Find the greatest speed at which the car can travel without slipping.
ms: friction provides the central force: μmg = mv²/60

exam.stem: A particle is released from rest at the top of a smooth fixed sphere of radius a and slides down its outside surface.

parts.q: Find the angle between the radius to the particle and the upward vertical when it leaves the surface.
ms: radial equation: mg cos θ − R = mv²/a

exam.stem: A particle of mass 0.3 kg is attached to a string of length 1.2 m whose other end is fixed. It moves in a horizontal circle with angular speed 4 rad s⁻¹.

parts.q: Find the tension in the string.
ms: T sin θ = m(l sin θ)ω², so T = mlω²

parts.q: Find the angle between the string and the vertical.

lessons.title: Centres of mass of particles, rods and laminae
notes: A centre of mass is a mass-weighted position: x̄=Σmᵢxᵢ/Σmᵢ. For a continuous body replace the sums by integrals with the appropriate density and area or length element. Symmetry can establish one coordinate, but only if the mass distribution has that symmetry.

For composite laminae, treat a removed region as negative mass at its own centre. Distinguish the geometric centre from the centre of mass of a non-uniform body. When integrating a rod, include its linear density in both the mass integral and the first moment.

example.q: A rod occupies 0≤x≤2 with linear density ρ(x)=kx, k>0. Find its centre of mass.
steps: The centre lies towards the denser right end.

practice.q: Particles of masses 2,3 and 5 kg lie at x=0,2 and 4 m. Find their centre of mass.

check.q: Find the centre-of-mass x-coordinate of equal masses at x=2 and x=8.

deep.tip: Split a composite body into simple parts, list each part’s mass (or area) and centre in a table, and take moments about a chosen axis; a removed part contributes a negative mass. For a region under a curve, use x̄ = ∫xy dx/∫y dx and ȳ = ½∫y² dx/∫y dx. A suspended body hangs with its centre of mass vertically below the point of suspension.

examples.title: A composite lamina
examples.q: An L-shaped lamina is made from a 6 × 2 rectangle along the x-axis (0 ≤ x ≤ 6, 0 ≤ y ≤ 2) and a 2 × 4 rectangle on top (0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 2 ≤ y ≤ 6). Find its centre of mass.

examples.title: A region under a curve
examples.q: Find the centre of mass of the uniform lamina bounded by y = x², the x-axis and x = 2.

examples.title: Hanging freely
examples.q: The L-shaped lamina in the first example is suspended from the origin. Find the angle between the edge along the x-axis and the vertical.
steps: The centre of mass (2.2, 2.2) hangs vertically below the origin.
The angle between the x-axis edge and the line to the centre of mass has tan θ = 2.2/2.2.

fills.q: Particles of 2 kg at x = 0 and 6 kg at x = 4.
A uniform rod from x = 0 to x = 8.

exam.stem: A uniform square lamina OABC has side 4 cm, with O at the origin and A at (4, 0). A square of side 2 cm in the corner 2 ≤ x ≤ 4, 2 ≤ y ≤ 4 is removed.

parts.q: Show that the centre of mass of the remaining lamina is at (5/3, 5/3).
The lamina is suspended from A and hangs in equilibrium. Find the angle between OA and the vertical.
ms: horizontal and vertical distances from A: 7/3 and 5/3

exam.stem: R is the region bounded by y = √x, the x-axis and the line x = 4.

parts.q: Find the coordinates of the centre of mass of a uniform lamina occupying R.
A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and mass 3 kg has particles of mass 1 kg at A and 2 kg at B. Find the distance of the centre of mass from A.

lessons.title: Rigid-body equilibrium, sliding and toppling
notes: A rigid body in equilibrium has zero resultant force and zero resultant moment. Choose a pivot that eliminates unknown forces where possible. At impending sliding use the limiting friction law F=μR; at impending toppling the resultant contact force acts through an edge.

Compare the conditions for both possible failures. A body does not necessarily topple just because a toppling angle has been calculated: it may slide first. The centre-of-mass projection must remain within the support base for static stability.

example.q: A uniform rectangular block has base width 0.6 m and height 0.8 m. Find the tilt angle at impending toppling on a rough plane, assuming no sliding.
steps: The centre is 0.3 m horizontally and 0.4 m vertically from the lower edge.
At toppling, the weight line passes through that edge.
The no-sliding assumption must be checked against friction if μ is supplied.

practice.q: A uniform block has base 0.4 m and height 1 m. Give the no-sliding toppling angle condition and the minimum μ to reach it without earlier sliding.
steps: The limiting sliding condition is tanθ=μ.
Require μ≥0.4 to avoid sliding before the toppling angle; equality is simultaneous.

check.q: A block has base 0.6 and height 0.8. Find tanθ at toppling, assuming no sliding.

deep.tip: Draw every force and take moments about a point that removes unknown forces, then resolve in two perpendicular directions. In limiting equilibrium friction equals μR, acting to oppose the impending motion. For a block on a slope, compare the angle for sliding (tan α = μ) with the angle for toppling (the weight’s line of action passes through the lower edge).

examples.title: A ladder against a smooth wall
examples.q: A uniform ladder of length 5 m and mass 20 kg rests against a smooth vertical wall at 60° to rough horizontal ground. It is about to slip. Find the coefficient of friction.
steps: Moments about the foot: S × 5 sin 60° = 20g × 2.5 cos 60°.
Resolving: F = S and R = 20g = 196 N.

examples.title: Slide or topple?
examples.q: A uniform block with base 0.5 m and height 1.2 m stands on a rough plane (μ = 0.6) whose angle is slowly increased. Does it slide or topple first?
steps: It would slide when tan α = μ = 0.6, at α = 31.0°.
It would topple when tan α = 0.5/1.2, at α = 22.6°.

fills.q: A force of 30 N at a perpendicular distance of 0.4 m.
A block of width 0.3 m and height 0.6 m.

exam.stem: A uniform ladder of length 4 m and mass 12 kg rests with its foot on rough horizontal ground and its top against a smooth vertical wall. The coefficient of friction is 0.4, and the ladder makes an angle α with the ground.

parts.q: Find the least value of tan α for which the ladder can rest in equilibrium.
ms: moments about the foot: S × 4 sin α = 12g × 2 cos α

parts.q: State how you have used the fact that the wall is smooth.
ms: the reaction at the wall is perpendicular to the wall: there is no friction there

exam.stem: A uniform rod AB of length 3 m and mass 10 kg is hinged to a vertical wall at A. It is held horizontal by a light string from B to the point C on the wall 2 m vertically above A.

parts.q: Find the tension in the string.
ms: perpendicular distance from A to BC: 3 × 2/√13

parts.q: A uniform cube rests on a rough plane with coefficient of friction 0.8. The angle of the plane is slowly increased. Determine whether the cube slides or topples first.

lessons.title: Variable resistance and simple harmonic motion
notes: Write the equation of motion with an explicit positive direction. If resistance depends on velocity, acceleration may be written dv/dt or v dv/dx according to the independent variable. A terminal velocity solves the zero-acceleration equation, but the full solution determines how it is approached.

Simple harmonic motion satisfies x″=−ω²x relative to an equilibrium position. Its period is 2π/ω and v²=ω²(A²−x²). The minus sign indicates restoring acceleration towards equilibrium. A spring system may require a shift from natural length to equilibrium extension before this form appears.

example.q: A particle satisfies x″=−9x, with x(0)=2 and x′(0)=0. Find x and the period.
steps: Velocity is −6sin3t, consistent with rest initially.

practice.q: A falling body obeys dv/dt=10−2v with v(0)=0. Find v(t) and terminal velocity.
steps: The equilibrium speed satisfies 10−2v=0, so v=5.
Solve the linear equation to obtain v=5+Ce^(−2t).

check.q: If x″=−9x, what is the period divided by π?

deep.tip: Write Newton’s second law with the right form of acceleration: dv/dt for force as a function of time, v dv/dx for force as a function of displacement, and separate the variables. For simple harmonic motion, identify ω from ẍ = −ω²x, then use v² = ω²(a² − x²), maximum speed aω, and period 2π/ω.

examples.title: A force varying with time
examples.q: A particle of mass 2 kg starts from rest at the origin and is acted on by a force of 6t N. Find its velocity and displacement at t = 2.
steps: v = 1.5t² (v = 0 at t = 0), so v(2) = 6 m s⁻¹.

examples.title: Resistance proportional to v²
examples.q: A boat of mass 200 kg cuts its engine at 10 m s⁻¹. The resistance is 8v² N. Find how far it travels before its speed halves.

examples.title: Simple harmonic motion
examples.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.5 m and period π s. Find its maximum speed and its speed 0.3 m from the centre.

fills.q: SHM with ω = 3 and amplitude 2 m.

exam.stem: A particle of mass 0.5 kg moves in a straight line. At time t seconds the resultant force on it is (4 − 2t) N. It starts from rest at the origin.

parts.q: Find the greatest speed of the particle in the first 4 seconds.
Find the distance travelled before the particle next comes to rest.

exam.stem: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion. Its maximum speed is 3 m s⁻¹ and its maximum acceleration is 12 m s⁻².

parts.q: Find the amplitude and the period of the motion.
Find the time taken to move from the centre to a point 0.375 m from the centre.

exam.stem: A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ freewheels so that its deceleration is 0.1v m s⁻².

parts.q: Find the time taken for its speed to fall to 5 m s⁻¹.
Find the distance travelled in this time.

lessons.title: Vector kinematics and projectiles
notes: Differentiate a vector position to obtain velocity and then acceleration; integrate with separate constants for each component. A force depending on time changes velocity through its time integral. Speed is the magnitude of velocity and is not obtained by adding its components.

For a projectile, resolve the initial velocity horizontally and vertically, apply the landing-height condition and select the physically relevant positive time. In three dimensions the horizontal projection can have two components, while gravity acts vertically. Check whether resistance is explicitly ignored and which vertical origin was chosen.

example.q: A particle has r(t)=(t²,3t,4−t²) m. Find velocity, acceleration and speed at t=1.

practice.q: A projectile starts at ground level with velocity (6,8) m/s in a vertical plane. With g=10 m/s² and no resistance, find flight time and horizontal range.
steps: Landing at y=0 gives t=0 or t=8/5.

check.q: For r(t)=(t²,3t,4−t²), find the y-component of velocity.

deep.tip: Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately: the horizontal component of velocity is constant, while the vertical motion has acceleration g downwards. For vector kinematics, differentiate r to get v and a, and integrate the other way, using the initial position or velocity to find each constant vector.

examples.title: A projectile from the ground
examples.q: A ball is projected from level ground at 25 m s⁻¹ at 40° above the horizontal. Find the time of flight, the range and the greatest height.
steps: Vertical: 0 = 25 sin 40° t − 4.9t², so t = 3.28 s.

examples.title: Integrating a velocity vector
examples.q: A particle has velocity v = 3t²i + (4 − 2t)j and is at (i + 2j) when t = 0. Find its position when it is moving parallel to i.
steps: r = (t³ + 1)i + (4t − t² + 2)j, using the initial position.
Parallel to i when the j-component of velocity is 0: 4 − 2t = 0.

examples.title: Horizontal projection from a cliff
examples.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from a cliff 40 m high. Find how far from the foot of the cliff it lands.

fills.q: Vertical component of the initial velocity 9.8 m s⁻¹.
lines: time of flight on level ground = [[2]] s

fills.q: Horizontal velocity 10 m s⁻¹ for 3 s.

exam.stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at an angle α above the horizontal, where tan α = ¾.

parts.q: Find the time of flight.
Find the horizontal range.
Find the length of time for which the ball is more than 5 m above the ground.

exam.stem: A particle moves with velocity v = (6t − 4)i + 3t²j m s⁻¹.

parts.q: Find the magnitude of its acceleration when t = 1.
Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 2.
A stone is projected from the top of a cliff 20 m above the sea, at 30 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find the horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff to where it lands.
ms: solves the quadratic and takes the positive root

lessons.title: Sorting, packing and graph terminology
notes: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps. State the version of a sorting or bin-packing algorithm, apply its tie-breaking rule consistently and show intermediate passes. An algorithm’s order describes how work grows with input size, not a fixed execution time.

A graph has vertices and edges; distinguish a path, cycle, tree and spanning tree. Planarity concerns whether a crossing-free drawing exists, not whether the current drawing has crossings. First-fit decreasing requires sorting before packing, and a feasible packing is not automatically optimal.

example.q: Use first-fit decreasing to pack items 6,5,4,3,2 into bins of capacity 10.
steps: Place 6 in bin 1 and 5 in bin 2.
Place 3 and then 2 in bin 2, now full.
Two bins are used; the total size is 20, so two is also a lower bound and the packing is optimal.

practice.q: Use first-fit decreasing for items 8,7,3,2 with capacity 10.
steps: Bin 1 starts with 8; bin 2 starts with 7.
Two bins suffice and total size 20 proves optimality.

check.q: Items total 20 and bin capacity is 10. What is the volume-based lower bound on bin count?

deep.tip: Carry out an algorithm exactly as stated and record each pass or comparison, because the marks are for the working as well as the result. For bin packing, find the lower bound (total ÷ capacity, rounded up) first, so you can tell whether a packing is optimal; for a binary search, use the middle position rounded up, and halve the list each time.

examples.title: A bubble sort
examples.q: Use a bubble sort to arrange 7, 3, 9, 4, 6 in ascending order, showing the result of each pass.
steps: Pass 1: swap 7 and 3; keep 7, 9; swap 9 and 4; swap 9 and 6. Result 3, 7, 4, 6, 9.
Pass 2: swap 7 and 4; swap 7 and 6. Result 3, 4, 6, 7, 9.

lessons.title: Minimum spanning trees and shortest paths
notes: Kruskal’s algorithm adds eligible edges in increasing weight order without creating a cycle. Prim’s algorithm grows one connected tree. A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex with minimum total weight; it does not minimise every journey from a chosen origin.

Dijkstra’s algorithm permanently labels the smallest tentative distance and requires non-negative edge weights. Floyd’s algorithm updates all-pairs distances by allowing intermediate vertices in a stated order. Record predecessors or route information as well as distances so the actual path can be recovered.

example.q: An undirected graph has AB=2, AC=5, BC=1, BD=4, CD=2. Find an MST and the shortest A–D route.
steps: Kruskal selects BC=1, AB=2 and CD=2 without a cycle.
For the A–D journey, A–B–C–D has length 2+1+2=5.
A–B–D has length 6 and A–C–D has length 7.
The shortest route is A–B–C–D of length 5.

practice.q: Why can a minimum spanning tree fail to contain a shortest route between a particular pair of vertices?
steps: An MST optimises total connection cost for all vertices.
A shortest path optimises one endpoint-to-endpoint journey.
Removing a cycle can discard a shortcut useful for that journey.
The two optimisation objectives are different.

check.q: How many edges does a spanning tree on 7 vertices have?

deep.tip: For a minimum spanning tree, Kruskal adds the cheapest edge that does not make a cycle, while Prim grows one tree from a start vertex (and works directly on a distance matrix). Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one vertex: record order of labelling, final labels and working values, then trace the route back from the destination.

lessons.title: Route inspection and travelling-salesperson bounds
notes: A connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit when every vertex has even degree. Route inspection duplicates paths to pair odd vertices at minimum additional cost, then finds a closed traversal of every original edge. When there are more than two odd vertices, compare complete pairings rather than greedily selecting one cheap pair.

A travelling-salesperson tour visits each vertex and returns to the start; it need not traverse every edge. Nearest-neighbour tours give upper bounds. A minimum-spanning-tree construction after deleting a vertex and adding its two cheapest incident edges can give a lower bound for a tour. Distinguish a proven optimum from matching or non-matching bounds.

example.q: A connected network has total edge weight 40 and exactly two odd vertices P and Q. Their shortest connecting path has weight 7. Find the shortest closed route-inspection length.
steps: Both odd degrees must be made even.

practice.q: A route-inspection network has edge total 60 and four odd vertices. The three complete-pairing costs are 12,15 and 9. Find the minimum closed route length.
steps: Choose the least complete pairing cost, 9.
Add this duplicated-path cost to the original edge total.

check.q: A route-inspection graph has edge total 40 and just two odd vertices with shortest connecting distance 7. Find the shortest closed tour length.

deep.tip: For route inspection, list the odd vertices, consider every complete pairing, and add the cheapest pairing to the total edge weight; if the route need not be closed, the start and finish should be odd vertices. For the travelling salesperson problem, an upper bound comes from a tour such as nearest neighbour, and a lower bound from a residual minimum spanning tree plus the two shortest edges at the deleted vertex.

examples.title: Four odd vertices
examples.q: A network has total weight 85 and odd vertices A, B, C, D with shortest distances AB 5, CD 8, AC 6, BD 9, AD 7, BC 4. Find the length of the shortest closed inspection route.
steps: Pairings: AB + CD = 13, AC + BD = 15, AD + BC = 11.
Repeat the cheapest pairing, AD and BC.

examples.title: Different start and finish
examples.q: For the same network, the route may start and finish at different vertices. Find the shortest possible route.
steps: Two odd vertices can be the start and the finish, so only one pair needs repeating.
Repeat the shortest single path, BC = 4.
Start at A and finish at D (or vice versa): length 85 + 4 = 89.

examples.title: Bounds for a travelling salesperson tour
examples.q: Distances: AB 8, AC 5, AD 9, AE 7, BC 6, BD 4, BE 10, CD 7, CE 3, DE 6. Find upper and lower bounds for the shortest tour.
steps: Nearest neighbour from A: A–C (5), C–E (3), E–D (6), D–B (4), B–A (8): upper bound 26.
Delete A: a minimum spanning tree of B, C, D, E is CE 3, BD 4, BC 6, total 13.
Add the two shortest edges from A: 5 + 7. Lower bound 25.
So 25 ≤ shortest tour ≤ 26; the tour of length 26 is in fact optimal.

lessons.title: Critical paths, floats and resource scheduling
notes: In an activity-on-arc model, arrows represent activities and vertices represent events. Dummy activities express precedence without consuming time or resources. A forward pass uses maxima to find earliest event times; a backward pass uses minima to find latest event times.

Total float for an activity from i to j is latest(j)−earliest(i)−duration. A critical path has zero total float throughout and determines the minimum project completion time under the precedence model. Resource limits can increase this completion time, so a critical-path calculation is not itself a feasible staff schedule.

example.q: Activities A and B start together and take 3 and 5 days. C takes 4 days after A. D takes 2 days after both B and C. Find project duration.
steps: A finishes at 3 and B at 5.
A–C–D is critical; B has 2 days of total float.

practice.q: A takes 4 days; B takes 3 days after A; C takes 6 days after A. D takes 2 days after both B and C. Find the duration and critical path.
steps: B finishes at 7 and C at 10.
D runs from day 10 to day 12.

check.q: An activity from event i to j has earliest(i)=3, latest(j)=10 and duration 4. Find total float.

deep.tip: Carry out the forward pass for early event times (take the largest incoming value) and the backward pass for late times (take the smallest outgoing value). An activity is critical when its total float, late finish − early start − duration, is zero; a lower bound for the number of workers is the total activity time divided by the project duration, rounded up.

examples.title: Early and late times
examples.q: A (3) and B (5) start the project. C (2) and D (4) follow A. E (3) follows B and C. F (2) follows D and E. Find the duration and the critical activities.
steps: Forward pass: C and D start at 3; E starts at max(5, 5) = 5; F starts at max(7, 8) = 8.
Backward pass: F 8–10; E late finish 8; D late finish 8; C late finish 5; B late finish 5; A late finish 3.
Floats: D has 1; A, B, C, E and F have 0. Critical paths A–C–E–F and B–E–F.

or it ensures each activity is uniquely defined by its start and end events

lessons.title: Formulating and solving linear programmes graphically
notes: Define decision variables with units, translate each resource limit into an inequality and specify non-negativity. A linear objective has parallel level lines. In a bounded feasible polygon, an optimum occurs at a vertex, or along an edge when the objective is parallel to it.

Continuous and integer solutions are different problems. Rounding a continuous optimum may violate constraints or lose the best integer choice. Check unboundedness and infeasibility rather than assuming every diagram has one optimal corner.

example.q: Maximise 3x+2y subject to x+y≤4, x≤2 and x,y≥0.
steps: Both x+y≤4 and x≤2 are active there.

practice.q: Maximise 2x+3y subject to x+y≤5, x≤3, y≤4 and x,y≥0.
steps: Check every listed point against the inequalities.

check.q: Evaluate objective 3x+2y at (2,2).

deep.tip: Define the decision variables with units, write the objective, then every constraint (including non-negativity). Draw the feasible region carefully and test the objective at each vertex, or slide an objective line; if the variables must be integers, check the integer points near the optimal vertex rather than rounding.

steps: Maximise 30x + 40y subject to 2x + 3y ≤ 120, 2x + y ≤ 80, x, y ≥ 0.
Make 30 of P and 20 of Q for a profit of £1700.

examples.title: A minimisation
examples.q: Minimise 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 6, x + 3y ≥ 12, x, y ≥ 0.
steps: The feasible region is unbounded, above both lines.

examples.q: Maximise 5x + 4y subject to 6x + 4y ≤ 24, x + 2y ≤ 6, with x and y non-negative integers.
steps: The continuous optimum is at (3, 1.5), with value 21.
Test nearby integer points: (3, 1) gives 19, (2, 2) gives 18, (4, 0) gives 20.
The integer optimum is x = 4, y = 0, value 20.
