lessons.title: Simplex pivots and the two-stage method
notes: The simplex method moves between basic feasible solutions. Introduce slack variables for ≤ constraints and follow one consistent objective-row convention. A positive pivot column uses the smallest eligible non-negative ratio to retain feasibility; zero or negative pivot entries do not enter that ratio test.

Artificial variables provide a starting basis when ordinary slacks do not. In phase I minimise their sum; a positive optimal artificial sum proves infeasibility. If the minimum is zero, remove artificial variables appropriately and restore the original objective for phase II. A pivot improving an objective is not proof of optimality until the stopping criterion is met.

example.q: For maximise 3x+2y with x+y≤4 and x≤2, explain the first pivot from the slack basis.
steps: With x entering, eligible ratios are 4/1=4 and 2/1=2.
The second row leaves; pivot there to obtain x=2 at y=0.
The basis remains feasible. Further improvement can reach x=2,y=2 and objective 10.

practice.q: A phase-I simplex calculation minimising the sum of artificial variables finishes at value 3. What does this imply?
steps: Artificial variables would all need to be zero for the original constraints to hold.
The original linear programme is infeasible.
It is not appropriate to proceed to an ordinary phase-II optimum.

check.q: For entering column entries 1,2 and right-hand sides 6,8, find the minimum eligible ratio.

deep.tip: Choose the pivot column with the most negative entry in the objective row, then the pivot row by the smallest non-negative ratio of value to pivot-column entry. Divide the pivot row by the pivot, clear the rest of the column, and stop when the objective row has no negative entries; read basic variables from the columns that are unit vectors.

examples.title: Two iterations to the optimum
examples.q: Use the simplex algorithm to maximise P = 2x + 3y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8 and 3x + 2y ≤ 12.
steps: Initial tableau with slacks s and t; P row (−2, −3, 0, 0 | 0). Pivot on the y column: ratios 8/2 = 4 and 12/2 = 6, so row 1.
After pivoting: y = 4 − ½x − ½s, and the P row becomes (−½, 0, 3/2, 0 | 12).
Pivot on the x column: ratios 4/½ = 8 and 4/2 = 2, so row 2.
Optimal: x = 2, y = 3, P = 13, with both slacks zero.

examples.title: A ≥ constraint
examples.q: Explain how the constraint x + y ≥ 3 is handled in the two-stage simplex method.
steps: Subtract a surplus variable: x + y − s = 3.
The origin then gives s = −3, which is not allowed, so add an artificial variable a: x + y − s + a = 3.
Stage 1 minimises the sum of the artificial variables.
If that minimum is 0 a feasible starting point has been found; if it is positive, the problem has no feasible solution.

fills.q: The final tableau of the first worked example.

lessons.title: Transportation and stepping-stone improvements
notes: A transportation table allocates supplies to meet demands at minimum total unit cost. Balance the totals, adding an appropriate dummy source or destination if necessary. The north-west corner method constructs a feasible allocation without consulting costs, so it does not establish optimality.

A stepping-stone loop alternates additions and subtractions through occupied cells. Its signed unit cost gives the improvement per unit moved; the smallest allocation on a subtracting corner limits the move. Degeneracy requires care with the basis so valid loops and optimality tests remain possible.

example.q: Supplies are 20,30; demands are 25,25; costs are [[2,5],[4,1]]. Find the north-west allocation and test its only unused cell.
steps: Introducing x₁₂ changes the cost per unit by 5−2+4−1=6.
The change is positive, so no cost reduction is possible through this loop.
This allocation is optimal for this 2×2 problem.

practice.q: Use supplies 20,30 and demands 25,25 with costs [[4,1],[2,5]]. Improve the north-west allocation.
steps: The unused-cell loop changes cost by 1−4+2−5=−6 per unit.
The new allocations are x₁₂=20, x₂₁=25, x₂₂=5.

check.q: Supplies are 20 and 30, and demands are 25 and 25. What is the total supply?

deep.tip: Balance supply and demand first (add a dummy with zero costs if necessary), then check the initial solution has m + n − 1 occupied cells. Find shadow costs from the occupied cells (Rᵢ + Kⱼ = cost), compute improvement indices for the empty cells, and enter the most negative one using a stepping-stone loop of alternating + and − cells.

examples.title: A north-west corner solution
examples.q: Supplies A 30, B 40, C 30; demands X 20, Y 45, Z 35; costs A: 8, 6, 10; B: 9, 12, 13; C: 14, 9, 16. Find the north-west corner solution and its cost.
steps: Five occupied cells = 3 + 3 − 1, so the solution is not degenerate.

examples.title: Improvement indices and one iteration
examples.q: Improve the solution in the previous example.
steps: Shadow costs: R_A = 0, K_X = 8, K_Y = 6, R_B = 6, K_Z = 7, R_C = 9.
Indices: AZ 3, BX −5, CX −3, CY −6; enter CY.
Loop CY+, BY−, BZ+, CZ−: θ = min(35, 30) = 30.
New solution: A X 20, Y 10; B Y 5, Z 35; C Y 30. Cost £1005 (recalculate the indices to test for optimality).

lessons.title: Hungarian allocation and linear programming models
notes: An assignment problem chooses one task per worker and one worker per task. In the Hungarian method for minimisation, reduce rows first and then columns. Cover all zeroes with the minimum number of lines; if too few independent zeroes exist, adjust the uncovered entries and doubly covered entries correctly.

For a maximum-profit problem, convert to a consistent minimisation table before applying the algorithm. Add dummy rows or columns when appropriate and interpret them in context. An assignment LP uses binary decision variables with row and column sums equal to one; do not confuse a table of reduced costs with the original total cost.

example.q: Minimise assignment cost for [[4,1,3],[2,0,5],[3,2,2]].
steps: Cover zeroes by column 2 and row 3. The smallest uncovered entry is 1.

practice.q: Find the minimum assignment cost for [[4,1],[2,5]].
steps: The minimum is 3, using worker 1→task 2 and worker 2→task 1.

check.q: For costs [[4,1],[2,5]], find the cost of the off-diagonal assignment.

deep.tip: Make the matrix square with a dummy row or column of zeros, and for a maximisation subtract every entry from the largest. Reduce rows then columns, cover the zeros with the fewest lines, and if fewer than n lines are needed adjust by the smallest uncovered value (subtract it from uncovered entries and add it where lines cross) before trying again.

examples.title: The Hungarian algorithm
examples.q: Find the minimum cost allocation for the cost matrix A: 10, 7, 8; B: 6, 9, 5; C: 8, 7, 8.
steps: Column reduction (column 1 minimum 1): A: 2, 0, 1; B: 0, 4, 0; C: 0, 0, 1.
Covering the zeros needs 3 lines (column 1, column 2, row B), so an allocation is possible.

examples.title: A maximisation

The Hungarian algorithm gives W₁–job 2, W₂–job 3, dummy–job 1.
Minimum cost 5 + 4 = 9; job 1 is not done.

lessons.title: Maximum flow, minimum cuts and restricted networks
notes: A feasible flow respects every arc capacity and conservation at intermediate vertices. Augment along a source-to-sink route in the residual network, whose backward arcs allow previous choices to be revised. A saturated-looking forward network alone does not prove maximality.

A cut separates source from sink and its directed capacity is the sum of forward arcs crossing that separation. The max-flow min-cut theorem proves optimality when a feasible flow matches a cut capacity. Multiple sources, vertex restrictions and lower bounds require appropriate network transformations before applying the standard algorithm.

example.q: A network has arcs s→a capacity 4, a→t capacity 3, s→b capacity 2 and b→t capacity 5. Find maximum flow.
steps: The cut with source side {s,a} has capacity 3+2=5.
Matching flow and cut proves a maximum of 5.

practice.q: A feasible network flow has value 12 and a source–sink cut has capacity 12. What can be concluded?
steps: Every feasible flow is at most the capacity of every source–sink cut.
Its value 12 is maximal and the cut is minimal.
Both feasibility and the directed cut calculation are essential.

check.q: A feasible flow of value 5 matches a cut capacity of 5. Find maximum flow.

deep.tip: A flow must satisfy capacities on every arc and conservation at every intermediate vertex. Find flow-augmenting routes until none remain, then prove maximality with a cut: by the max-flow min-cut theorem, a flow equal to the capacity of a cut is maximal. Count only arcs directed from the source side to the sink side when finding a cut’s capacity.

examples.title: Augmenting and a cut
examples.q: Arcs: SA 10, SB 8, AB 3, AC 6, BD 9, CT 7, DT 8, CD 4. Find the maximum flow from S to T.
steps: Augment S–A–C–T by 6 and S–B–D–T by 8: flow 14.
Any further route must use CT or DT, but DT is full and C can only receive 6.
The cut separating {S, A, B, D} from {C, T} has capacity AC + DT = 6 + 8 = 14.
Flow 14 = cut 14, so the maximum flow is 14.

examples.title: Several sources
examples.q: Sources S₁ (supply 15) and S₂ (supply 10) feed A and B: S₁A 9, S₁B 8, S₂B 7, AT 12, BT 11. Find the maximum flow.
steps: Add a supersource S with arcs SS₁ 15 and SS₂ 10.
Through A at most 9 (only S₁ feeds it); through B at most min(11, 8 + 7) = 11.
Maximum flow 9 + 11 = 20; the cut through S₁A and BT has capacity 9 + 11 = 20, confirming it.

fills.q: Arcs from the source side: 6 and 8.
A flow of 12 and a cut of capacity 12.

replace the vertex by two vertices joined by an arc with the vertex capacity

lessons.title: Dynamic programming and Bellman recursions
notes: A staged optimisation problem uses states that contain all information needed for future choices. Define a value function for the best remaining cost or reward. Work backwards from the final stage, choosing the minimum or maximum over feasible next decisions.

Record the decision attaining each value as well as the value itself, then trace a route forwards. A greedy choice based only on the next edge can fail because the remaining cost differs by destination. Avoid mixing a minimisation recurrence with a maximisation terminal condition.

example.q: From S choose A at cost 2 or B at cost 5. From A to T costs 8; from B to T costs 1. Find the cheapest route.
steps: Choose S–B–T, even though its first edge costs more.

practice.q: S→A costs 4, S→B costs 1, A→T costs 2 and B→T costs 7. Use a backward recurrence.
steps: A locally cheapest first edge would be misleading.

check.q: Two candidate route costs are 2+8 and 5+1. Find their minimum.

deep.tip: Work backwards from the final stage, recording at each state the best value so far and the action that achieves it. The objective may be a minimum total, a maximum total, a minimax (smallest largest stage value) or a maximin (largest smallest stage value), so state which before starting; then trace the optimal decisions forwards from the start.

lessons.title: Zero-sum games, dominance and mixed strategies
notes: A payoff table must specify whose gain is shown. The row player maximises and the column player minimises that payoff in a zero-sum model. If maximin equals minimax, a saddle point gives an optimal pure strategy. Dominated strategies can be removed only with the correct inequality direction.

For a 2×2 game without a saddle point, make the opponent indifferent between the relevant pure responses to find a mixed strategy. Check that the probabilities lie between zero and one. Larger games may be solved graphically or with a linear-programming formulation, with probabilities summing to one.

example.q: The row player’s payoffs are [[3,0],[1,2]]. Find optimal mixing probabilities and game value.
steps: Row minima are 0,1; column maxima are 3,2, so there is no saddle point.
If row 1 is used with probability p, column payoffs are 1+2p and 2−2p.
If column 1 is used with probability q, row payoffs are 3q and 2−q.

practice.q: Find the mixed strategy for the row player in the game [[2,0],[0,4]].
steps: If row 1 has probability p, the two column responses give 2p and 4−4p.

check.q: For payoffs [[3,0],[1,2]], solve 1+2p=2−2p for row mixing probability p.

deep.tip: Check for a saddle point first: if the largest row minimum equals the smallest column maximum, both players should play safe. Otherwise remove dominated strategies, then for a 2 × n game plot the row player’s expected gain against p for each column and choose p at the highest point of the lower boundary.

examples.title: A stable solution
examples.q: Find the play-safe strategies for the game with row payoffs R1: 4, 2, 5; R2: 1, 1, 0; R3: 6, 2, 3.
steps: Row minima 2, 0, 2: the row player’s maximin is 2 (R1 or R3).
Column maxima 6, 2, 5: the column player’s minimax is 2 (C2).
Maximin = minimax = 2, so there is a saddle point.
Play safe: R1 or R3 against C2; value 2.

examples.title: A 2 × 3 game
examples.q: Row payoffs: R1: 3, −1, 2; R2: −2, 4, 1. Find the row player’s optimal mixed strategy and the value.
steps: Let R1 be played with probability p. Expected gains: C1: 5p − 2; C2: 4 − 5p; C3: p + 1.
The row player maximises the least of these lines.
The lowest boundary is highest where 5p − 2 = 4 − 5p, so p = 0.6 (and then C3 gives 1.6 ≥ 1).
Play R1 with probability 0.6 and R2 with 0.4; value 1.

examples.title: Dominance
examples.q: Reduce the game R1: 3, 1, 4; R2: 2, 0, 3; R3: 5, 2, 1 using dominance.
steps: Every entry of R1 exceeds the matching entry of R2.
So R1 dominates R2, and R2 can be removed.
The game reduces to R1: 3, 1, 4; R3: 5, 2, 1, which has the same value.

lessons.title: Recurrence models and long-run behaviour
notes: A recurrence specifies the timing of an update. In a population or savings model, multiplying before adding is different from adding before multiplying. Write the update in words and identify the initial index before solving the algebraic recurrence.

For uₙ₊₁=auₙ+b, an equilibrium is b/(1−a) when a≠1. Deviations multiply by a each step, so |a|<1 gives convergence, while |a|>1 generally gives growing deviations. A formal limit must also be consistent with any physical restrictions of the model.

example.q: Solve uₙ₊₁=0.8uₙ+10 with u₀=0 and find its limit.

practice.q: A quantity obeys uₙ₊₁=0.5uₙ+6 with u₀=4. Find uₙ and its limit.

check.q: Find the equilibrium L satisfying L=0.8L+10.

deep.tip: Identify the order and the type before solving: a first-order recurrence uₙ₊₁ = auₙ + b has a constant particular solution b/(1 − a) when a ≠ 1, and second-order linear recurrences use the auxiliary equation. Always check one value from the recurrence, and interpret the long-term behaviour (the limit exists when |a| < 1).

lessons.title: Decision trees, conditional information and expected value
notes: A decision tree separates decision nodes from chance nodes. Work backwards: average at a chance node using conditional probabilities and select the best expected value at a decision node. Subtract costs at the stage where they occur; do not count them twice.

Expected value is a model-based long-run criterion, not a guarantee for one outcome. The expected value of perfect information compares the best decision in each known state with the best current decision. For imperfect sample information, use the correct updated conditional probabilities before choosing an action.

example.q: A fictional product earns 100 units in a good market and loses 40 in a bad market. P(good)=0.6. Not launching gives 0. Find the expected value of perfect information.
steps: Without information, choose launch with EV 44.
With perfect information, launch only in a good market.
The value of perfect information is 60−44=16 units.

practice.q: A fictional launch gains 50 units with probability 0.7 and loses 20 otherwise. Not launching gives 0. Find the expected value of perfect information.
steps: With perfect information, act only in the favourable state: EV=35.

check.q: Find the expected value of 100 with probability 0.6 and −40 otherwise.

deep.tip: Draw the tree from left to right with decision nodes (squares) and chance nodes (circles), and put payoffs at the ends. Roll back from right to left: at a chance node take the expected value; at a decision node choose the best branch and mark the rejected branches. The expected value of perfect information is the expected value with perfect information minus the best expected monetary value without it.
